talks.title: TR19: NAT64 Day 2019 @ AWK
talks.teaser: An enterprise practitioner documents NAT64 and DNS64 tests that put managed clients on IPv6-only LANs against IPv4-only internal services.
talks.summary:
The presenter describes experiments at AWK Group to place managed Windows clients on an IPv6-only network while most internal applications and trust-zone resources remain on IPv4. Motivation is hands-on validation: whether the approach is feasible, how hard the setup is, and whether it can replace dual stack for that use case.

A separate Juniper SRX acts as NAT64 gateway with static, stateless one-to-one NAT so outbound and inbound sessions map predictably—important when deployment tools must reach clients. DNS synthesis relies on Juniper DNS doctoring (RFC 6147) rather than a dedicated DNS64 server. Lab testing across Zurich and branch sites shows strong results for file shares, SharePoint, RDP, Skype for Business, printing, Outlook, and many consulting tools; failures include Active Directory dynamic DNS registration, inbound Microsoft Teams calls, and unstable VMware Horizon desktop display. A planned company-wide cutover stops after a ten-client pilot; guest Wi-Fi runs IPv6-only for three hours, surfacing Android flapping, SMS verification quirks, and Windows router-advertisement behavior differences between Ethernet and Wi-Fi.

Practitioners should expect a straightforward firewall configuration but must plan for bidirectional reachability, policy ordering on Juniper (IPv6-to-IPv4 rules), VPN split tunneling that sends DNS to IPv4-only resolvers, and application dependencies on literal IPv4 addresses outside DNS doctoring’s scope.

talks.title: TR19: IPv666 - Address of the Beast
talks.teaser: Explains why scanning IPv6 is hard and how a probability-based tool finds live hosts at scale.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why scanning IPv6 is hard, given the enormous address space and privacy extensions that randomize host bits so addresses change over time. The speakers first ran a honeypot fed by paid ad traffic, which collected about 92 thousand unique addresses for roughly 1,200 dollars, but most of those clients used ephemeral addresses and were offline when scanned. A machine learning autoencoder approach failed, so they built a simpler per-nibble probability model that initially produced around 50,000 responsive addresses from 10 million generated candidates.

The biggest problem was alias networks, where an entire range answers from a single machine and pollutes the model's feedback loop. The team detected aliasing by probing random addresses inside a /96 and then used a binary search to locate the boundary of the aliased range. They then adapted a clustering algorithm from a 2017 paper into a faster version and added neighborhood expansion, varying nibbles of discovered addresses and walking adjacent /64 networks.

In the version 0.3 release, a one-hour scan throttled to 50 megabits per second found 1.57 million live addresses, with 78% absent from existing datasets. A TCP check of 100,000 of them showed common services such as SSH, telnet, web servers and networking equipment. The toolset, called ipv6 66, requires Go 1.11 or later and runs only on Linux. The main takeaway is that IPv6 addresses are not hidden just because the space is large, so exposed services should not rely on obscurity.

talks.title: TR19: SI6 IPv6 Toolkit v3.0
talks.teaser: The session demos SI6 v3 tools for IPv6 recon: Bing domain harvesting, certificate transparency queries, and throw-address rotation.
talks.summary:
IPv6 network reconnaissance cannot lean on the same address brute-forcing approaches that work in IPv4, so gathering host and domain visibility requires alternate data sources. The presenter walks through three major additions in version 3.0 of the SI6 IPv6 toolkit, emphasizing capabilities that had not been shown in prior releases.

One component scrapes search-engine results—primarily Bing—with language dictionaries and optional drill-down into subdomains, and pairs that workflow with manually created ephemeral IPv6 addresses on a delegated /48 prefix so many parallel instances can run on one host without hitting per-address result caps. A second tool queries certificate transparency logs (with wildcard support) to list SSL-enabled names, including mail and other hosts that search indexes miss; when log interfaces cap bulk downloads, the toolkit splits zones by label count and pipes partitioned names from the search-engine helper. The third tool, Messi, orchestrates search scraping, transparency lookups, DNS record checks, and IPv6 reverse enumeration while deduplicating work, with optional domain and prefix filters for scoped assessments.

Practitioners gain concrete patterns for building domain and address inventories over IPv6, combining complementary leaks from indexes and public certificate logs, and automating chained enumeration instead of repeating manual steps.

talks.title: TR19: NGI
talks.teaser: Explains how outsiders attack autonomous vehicles by jamming or spoofing GPS, lidar, cameras, radar, and maps without platform access.
talks.summary:
The presentation argues that autonomous and connected unmanned vehicles belong on the same risk map as other IoT devices, except their mass makes flawed perception or planning physically dangerous. It deliberately avoids ordinary network intrusion and instead catalogs what an attacker can do from outside by breaking or lying to sensors and by abusing maps and V2V-style messaging assumptions.

Failure stories anchor the technical thread. A DARPA Grand Challenge frontrunner trusted lidar over a pre-recorded GPS path and crashed; a fatal Tesla Autopilot case hinged on lane markings versus following the car ahead. The speaker maps vehicle software as stacked real-time control, collision avoidance, navigation, and mission logic, then walks common sensing modalities. GPS can be jammed or spoofed with inexpensive SDR gear, including demonstrations that force consumer drones into no-fly landings. Lidar faces denial, reflectivity tricks, forged lane paint, and active relay spoofing through curved housings. Cameras, millimeter-wave radar, IMUs, wheel encoders, and parking ultrasonics each get practical abuse patterns, with map data and fake traffic lights as additional leverage.

Connected-vehicle standards (DSRC, unencrypted but certificate-authenticated BSM traffic) and flawed traffic-sensor deployments are contrasted with a slow civilian rollout timeline. A Manhattan traffic-modeling example shows how hacking only a few vehicles per lane-kilometer can isolate most streets. The closing emphasis is building adversarial thinking into design before fleets harden around weak assumptions.

Leandro Cortés details critical flaws in widely deployed 433 MHz vehicle and home alarm ecosystems sold globally by vendors he cannot legally name, showing how fixed codewords and simplistic state machines break even when marketing promises proprietary press-code technology. Using a twenty-dollar RTL-SDR and Arduino-class transmitters, he captures remote signals, decodes bit timings, and reproduces activation, deactivation, and denial-of-service floods that drain panels and batteries.

Live motorcycle and car demos include replay and "code knocking" sequences that bypass validators, while a second supplier requires only a single captured frame for replay. A Canadian wireless home panel variant is trivially bypassed with one sniffed remote command. He urges buyers to treat consumer RF alarms as untrusted and questions insurer evidence after silent thefts.

talks.title: TR19: Keynote - Inside the Machine
talks.teaser: The keynote connects mitigation skepticism, exploit primitive formalization, and encrypted-memory attacks to practical defense engineering.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by critiquing how security discourse swings between treating every bug as catastrophic and treating every mitigation as a silver bullet, and urges the audience to use shared arguments rather than unstated common sense. He contrasts mature threat modeling with vague “raise the bar” claims, proposes demanding that class mitigations demonstrably stop multiple real instances, and insists that anyone designing mitigations must understand exploitation—ideally by building exploits on modern systems or partnering with those who have.

The middle of the talk ties formalization efforts (including LangSec, heap modeling, and published exploit-primitive work) to gaps in reproducibility, metrics, and lost exploit metadata. He revisits memory encryption as a widespread reality, introduces a non-oblivious attacker who learns from encrypted memory changes, and walks through prior Linux pre-authentication bypass logic and a brute-force corruption path against kernel credential fields, including a VM demo that eventually sets effective UID to zero.

Practitioners should leave with three anchors: prove mitigations against concrete vulnerability instances before permanent complexity accumulates; treat a working exploit as the definitive proof of understanding before advocating fixes; and let defensive investment follow and reuse serious offensive research rather than presentations alone.

talks.title: TR19: MS Office file format sorcery
talks.teaser: Shows how macro-enabled Office files slip past static and dynamic analysis via format spec gaps and undocumented P-code.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why Office macros remain a common entry point for attackers, and why red teams need ways past both static and dynamic analysis. The speakers first walk through the compound file binary format that Office uses, where the VBA project storage holds module streams with compressed source code and an uncompressed performance cache of P-code. They then show how small deviations from the published specification can make common parsers fail or report the wrong code.

In the demonstrations, a basic Cobalt Strike macro dropped from 34 detections on VirusTotal to 29 after an extra byte was appended to the compressed section, and some major engines stopped flagging it. Hiding the macro from the editor meant changing the project stream. Replacing the visible source with fake code left the real P-code to run, which the analysis tools did not treat as the executed logic. Mismatched Unicode and MBCS stream names broke some analysis tools while Office still ran the code. Matching the target Office version was done by having a template fetched from a URL reveal the build.

The second part covers the scanning hooks in Office 365, where only behavior events for selected API calls are forwarded to the antivirus engine. Trusted locations, calls that are not trigger events, Excel 4 macros, simulated keystrokes and startup files that disable scanning were all shown as ways around it. The speakers also found that trusted document records could be reused for long-term persistence. They close by advising practitioners to look for ambiguity in specs, undocumented features and deviations from the spec, and note that other Office applications may be worth testing too.

talks.title: TR19: Fun and Pitfalls in a World of VDSL
talks.teaser: Maps everyday VDSL links from home routers through DSLAMs to operator systems and shows how to rebuild that chain in a cheap lab.
talks.summary:
The presentation argues that VDSL and the customer-premises gear behind it sit in a blind spot: most people never observe authentication between a home router and the operator, or how modern voice-over-IP calls are protected. It walks the chain from CPE and the DSLAM that terminates copper lines to operator dial-up, TR-069 auto-configuration, and IMS-style telephony, framed as infrastructure people trust without inspecting.

The core is a split lab—emulated provider back end with PPPoE and ACS services, VLAN plumbing that mirrors real carriers, an affordable Linux-based DSLAM, and an attacker VM for lawful middleperson testing. TR-069 is described as callback-driven XML where routers pull configuration, complicating direct fuzzing unless automation watches device health. Case studies cover several German-market xDSL boxes: legacy Vodafone Easybox provisioning with hard-coded material and short MIC guessing; resale routers still holding prior subscribers’ credentials; passive captures on a live O2 line showing PAP dial-in and odd SIP behavior; Telekom Speedport models including DHCP-only management paths, distinctive DNS casing, and signed firmware lists; and a newer Telekom unit that uses encrypted client certificates to the ACS until UART access during prep work yielded a root shell, SQLite configuration, and plaintext operator callback credentials.

The close emphasizes that none of this is occult IP engineering—Wireshark, Burp, and familiar tools suffice—but physical access still matters, especially shared building telephone entry points in Germany where an adversary could tap many tenants. Listeners leave with a parts list, VLAN pitfalls called out explicitly, and incentives to probe their own access networks defensively.

They recap historical milestones, present a Mirai-lineage case study, and close with live smart-home hacking demos underscoring weak default credentials and updaters.  Metrics cite Telnet backdoors, UPnP reflections, and consumer router APIs that bot herders weaponized after Mirai source code leaked.  Q&A invites operators to segment IoT VLANs and disable WAN administration on CPE even after botnet takedowns.

talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for TR19: Medical Device Security - Please (don't) be patient!.
talks.summary:
Julian Zuleta frames hospital environments as specialty operations where uptime beats hardening, then walks through EU and US medical-device regulation shifts such as the incoming EU MDR rules that finally ask for basic cybersecurity evidence. He contrasts that landscape with NHS WannaCry impacts and German BSI observations about missing authentication and home-grown crypto on networked clinical gear.

Case studies stay high level but concrete: misconfigured vital-sign monitors with impossible heart-rate thresholds, radiology workstations on aging Windows releases caching domain credentials in plaintext, unauthenticated root telnet on networked infusion pumps, and MRI fleets exposing multi-port services from patient Wi-Fi. Manufacturer excuses he cites include claiming telnet is knowingly unsafe yet shipping custom interpreters anyway.

Recommendations highlight FDA drafts on cybersecurity bills of materials, German BSI lifecycle guidance, CVSS limitations for patient-harm scenarios, and ERNW's upcoming BSI-funded testing project to publish plain-language device risk summaries for lay readers.

talks.title: TR19: Sneaking Past Device Guard
talks.teaser: Bypass paths against Windows Device Guard span Office macros, Excel 4.0 macros, and unpatched ActiveScript host behavior.
talks.summary:
Windows Device Guard applies certificate- and hash-based application whitelisting so that, after initial foothold, attackers cannot load arbitrary native code or use unrestricted PowerShell and ActiveScript. The presentation argues that many practical bypasses are not tracked as CVEs yet still defeat real adversaries who will abuse whatever native surface remains.

Techniques include VBA macros (outside Device Guard instrumentation), remote Office DCOM macro injection via AccessVBOM registry changes, adding user-writable HKCU trusted locations to drop macro execution out of protected mode, Excel 4.0 CALL and REGISTER macros with embedded x86 shellcode, ActiveScriptEventConsumer for WMI persistence, XSLT transforms through MSXML and Office, and forcing JScript 9 under CScript or scriptlet hosts so neither engine nor host invokes IsClassAllowed—a gap that received a November patch but leaves inconsistent host responsibilities. Chakra-driven Wscript.CreateObject is noted as an AMSI bypass on non–Device Guard systems.

Defenders are told that most activity surfaces in command lines, loaded DLLs, and registry changes, including Device Guard being disabled by admins. The speaker urges tightening Office on guarded endpoints, monitoring diverse bypass classes, and consistent COM enforcement across scripting hosts and languages.

talks.title: TR19: macOS - Gaining root with harmless AppStore apps
talks.teaser: Traces how an App Store installer's symlink handling let a standard user plant files that run as root on macOS.
talks.summary:
The talk began with a search for dylib hijacking in one application, which only turned up cases where placing a library required root. It recapped the two forms of dylib hijacking on macOS: missing libraries loaded by path, and @rpath lookups that search a sequence of locations. Microsoft replied that the root requirement was not a security bug. Checking the ownership of App Store, package and drag-and-drop installs raised the question of whether a standard admin user could get around that requirement.

The central finding is that a regular user can delete an App Store app from Launchpad without elevation, recreate its folders in /Applications, and reinstall it, so the installer writes into a location the user controls. The installer also follows symbolic links, which can redirect writes elsewhere, but filenames come from the package, so overwriting protected or existing files with chosen names did not work. The speaker built a free crontab editor for the App Store and used its bundled cron job files to get a root terminal on High Sierra. Package payloads could also be altered, but signatures and Gatekeeper block changed packages by default.

Recommendations include stopping the installer from following symlinks, refusing to install over an existing folder not owned by root, checking file counts in app bundles, and having paid apps verify purchases. The route no longer worked on Mojave, though the speaker said the fix was not the one wanted. How Launchpad tracks which apps came from the App Store was left as an open question.

talks.title: TR19: The Anatomy of Windows Telemetry
talks.teaser: Maps the architecture, data sources and network behaviour of Windows 10 telemetry and how to reduce it.
talks.summary:
Researchers from Germany's Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) examine the telemetry built into Windows 10. The analysis is part of a larger BSI project and uses a Windows 10 1607 Long Term Servicing Branch build, chosen for its feature stability over a multi-year project. The speakers explain why telemetry matters for confidentiality and integrity, especially for government clients where Windows 10 is set to become the standard client image.

The architecture centres on the Diagnostic Tracking Service. It gathers data from Event Tracing for Windows as the primary source and from bundled executables and API functions as secondary sources. Collected events are compressed, buffered and copied to a local transaction file before being uploaded to Microsoft-managed back-end hosts roughly every 10 to 15 minutes, while the service polls for updates on a fixed interval. The telemetry level and control files pushed by Microsoft determine which data collection points are enabled and which external executables run, and the trigger logic stays opaque. The team found a man-in-the-middle weakness in the HTTP handling that Microsoft has since fixed.

To reduce exposure, the speakers compare four options: lowering the telemetry level, blocking back-end endpoints, disabling the service, and isolating the machine from the internet. They rate each by how much data it removes, how sustainable it is and how much maintenance it needs. Blocking endpoints and tuning individual data collection points are not sustainable, because updates can change endpoints and components. They advise a risk assessment and disabling telemetry where it is not needed, and they outline future work: a richer data viewer and continuous analysis of the secondary data sources.

LDAP remains the source of truth for adminCount, nested domain admins, SPNs, and unconstrained delegation, while manual filters beat noisy net commands.

He releases krbroot for blazing Kerberos pre-auth spraying with minimal UDP traffic that often misses classic 4625 logging unless Kerberos auditing is enabled. The talk demos AS-REP roasting, overpass-the-hash via keytabs, ticket forging for persistence, and SMB/LDAP authenticated purely from .ccache files.

The goal is showing you do not need PowerShell on-domain to map and attack AD as long as DNS, time sync, and valid creds exist.

talks.teaser: Shows a PowerShell client that queries BloodHound's REST API, turning attack-path data into lists, metrics and reports.
talks.summary:
CypherDog is a PowerShell module that wraps the BloodHound REST API, so Active Directory attack-path data can be queried from the command line instead of through the web interface. The talk opens with a short recap of BloodHound's core vocabulary: nodes, edges and paths, plus the object and relationship types added over time, such as ACLs, GPO links and delegation.

The demonstrations focus on reading and changing graph data. Commands return nodes, edges and shortest or all paths as PowerShell objects, support tab completion and pipeline chaining, and can print the equivalent Cypher query for any call. The speaker also showed adding and editing nodes and edges, safety switches for deletions, per-object notes, and a cheapest-path option that weights edges other than group membership. Listing commands expose nested administrative rights, and counting commands rank nodes by memberships, local admins or sessions.

The final part covered metrics meant for management. A custom index measures what share of users can reach a high-value group and how many computers they can then access, alongside average hop counts. The talk closed with a node blacklisting approach for excluding paths, and a note that the code and a beta would be shared publicly. The main takeaway is that exporting graph results into tables and CSV files makes attack-path findings easier to quantify and explain to non-technical audiences.

talks.title: TR19: Active Directory and Azure
talks.teaser: Explains tiered administration, clean source and trust hardening for Active Directory and Azure hybrid environments.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the premise that Active Directory holds the keys to an organisation, that stolen credentials are a leading breach pattern, and that prevention alone is unrealistic in large environments, so containment becomes the goal. The speakers present three common core controls for a single forest: administrative tiering with logon and control restrictions, the clean source principle applied to administration, and attack path analysis with tools such as BloodHound to reveal hidden privileges and shadow admins.

The discussion then extends these controls to multi-forest and hybrid setups. For trusts, it argues that every trust affects security regardless of direction, and recommends unidirectional trusts, keeping SID filtering enabled, using selective authentication and reviewing trust configuration regularly. For Azure AD Connect, it notes that the default sync account can hold replication rights that allow a DCSync and reset most user passwords, so it should be hardened and placed under tier 0 control. ADFS servers and the pass-through authentication agent are also treated as tier 0 systems, because a stolen token signing key enables forged SAML logons to cloud services.

For Azure, the speakers suggest mapping tenant administrator roles into tiers, since a few roles can take over the whole tenant. Their recommendations include separating on-premises and cloud administration, requiring MFA on privileged roles, using conditional access tied to managed devices, and avoiding personal email addresses on cloud global administrator accounts. They also warn that marketplace VM images may be outdated. The practical takeaway is to classify every asset into exactly one tier, restrict logons and control paths between tiers, and check configurations on a schedule.

talks.title: TR19: BloodHound and the Adversary Resilience Methodology
talks.teaser: Shows how BloodHound queries expose Active Directory permissions, GPO control and admin paths that defenders can audit and remove.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Andrew Robbins and Rohan discuss how defenders can leverage BloodHound—historically an offensive Active Directory (AD) permissions mapping tool—to improve enterprise AD security posture through graph-based analysis. Grounded in John Lambert's quote that 'defenders think in lists, attackers think in graphs,' the speakers present practical auditing methodologies, real-world case studies, and new analytical tooling designed to identify and eliminate systemic attack paths.

### Key Topics
- **BloodHound 2.1 Release Features**: Recent additions include support for resource-based constrained delegation (using the `msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity` attribute and Will Schroeder's Rubeus research), an edge UI for exploitation and abuse info, a database warm-up button to load graphs into Neo4j RAM, optimized Cypher queries, improved data ingestion speed, and SharpHound collector updates (such as improved ACL parsing logic and detection fallback).
- **Active Directory Auditing via Graphs**: Using Cypher queries in Neo4j to audit complex permissions, including inbound AD object control (who can control Domain Admins), Group Policy Object (GPO) abuse paths (non-DA principals controlling GPOs linked to DAs), and least-privilege violations (identifying hosts with thousands of local admins).
- **Eliminating Stale Object Control (PrivExchange Case Study)**: Addressing excessive AD permissions granted by default Exchange installations. Exchange servers often inherit `WriteDacl` rights over the domain head from legacy installers (e.g., Exchange Server 2003), allowing attackers to perform DCSync. The speakers outline how to safely remove these permissions by deploying targeted System Access Control Lists (SACLs) and monitoring for Windows Event 5136.
- **Cross-Domain and Forest Attack Paths**: Demonstrating that Active Directory domain trusts are not security boundaries. Organizations often suffer from foreign local administrators and cross-domain group nesting, allowing low-privileged domain users to pivot through multiple trusts to forest-level compromise.
- **BloodHound Analytics Tooling**: The introduction of two open-source (GPLv3) tools to measure and monitor AD resilience: a Power BI workbook (`BloodHoundAnalytics.pbix`) and a QA verification script (`bloodhound_analytics.py`).

### Technical Details
- **Auditing GPOs**: Manual enumeration requires tracing linked OUs, inheritance blocks, WMI filters, and GUID lookups in ADUC. BloodHound maps these relationships natively, allowing single Cypher queries to isolate foreign groups or users with write/edit access to GPOs affecting Domain Admins.
- **SACL Validation Workflow**: To address fears that revoking dangerous permissions will cause operational outages, defenders can configure an auditing ACE in the target object's SACL (such as success auditing on the `modify_permissions` right for the Exchange Trusted Subsystem). If no Event 5136 is generated over a chosen evaluation period (e.g., 14 months in the speakers' client case), the corresponding discretionary ACE (`WriteDacl`) can be safely deleted without breaking service functionality.
- **BloodHound Analytics Suite**:
  - `BloodHoundAnalytics.pbix`: Connects directly to Neo4j to generate visual dashboards, highlighting metrics such as the percentage of users with an attack path to Domain Admin, high-risk groups, and distributions of local admin rights across endpoints.
  - `bloodhound_analytics.py`: Performs data completeness quality checks (noting that most environments only capture ~5% of user sessions), audits universal critical asset risks (e.g., RDP or local admin rights on Domain Controllers), and maps cross-domain exposure.

### Takeaways
Defenders cannot secure modern Active Directory environments using traditional flat lists and static spreadsheets. By viewing AD relationships as an attack graph, blue teams can locate critical bottleneck permissions, safely validate revocation through Windows event SACLs, and systematically sever attack paths before adversaries can exploit them.

talks.title: TR19: You (dis)liked mimikatz? Wait for kekeo
talks.teaser: Shows how Kekeo abuses Kerberos, CredSSP single sign-on and smart card certificates to obtain user credentials.
talks.summary:
The talk traces the history of mimikatz, the Windows credential tool, from early experiments with bypassing software restrictions to a toolkit that pulls credentials from memory. The speaker covers features added over the years, including cleartext password recovery, Kerberos ticket handling, golden and silver tickets, and modules touching event logging and DPAPI. The speaker explains that Kekeo was written because mimikatz does not handle network protocols, so a separate tool was needed for Kerberos and authentication at the protocol level.

The middle of the talk focuses on the CredSSP-based single sign-on used by Remote Desktop. The speaker shows that credentials sent to a terminal server can be captured by impersonating that server, and that a local administrator on the server can recover them without running as admin. The talk then turns to smart cards and PKINIT, showing how a certificate's private key can be used ahead of time to sign authentication timestamps and later obtain tickets. The speaker demonstrates this against a domain controller, and a separate demo shows that a delegated Kerberos ticket can be reused on another machine.

The closing section covers defensive takeaways. Windows ticket handling is restrictive by default, but delegation settings and certificate authority servers need strict protection, since a compromised PKI server can issue certificates for any user. The speaker notes that Microsoft's mitigations are opt-in and need recent Windows versions across the network, which many environments cannot meet. Protecting CA keys with HSMs and non-exportable configuration is presented as a practical measure.

talks.title: TR19: Not A Security Boundary: Breaking Forest Trusts
talks.teaser: Shows how a two-way forest trust with default settings lets an attacker in one forest compromise a partner forest.
talks.summary:
The talk challenges the long-held view that an Active Directory forest is a security boundary. The speakers start with Kerberos basics, ticket granting tickets, the three delegation models, and how domain trusts pass referral tickets between domains. They explain that SID filtering is meant to stop a trusted forest from abusing another forest, and they note that Microsoft documentation describes forests as security boundaries.

The core attack chains three default behaviours. A server with unconstrained delegation caches the TGTs of users who authenticate to it. The printer bug (the MS-RPRN print spooler RPC method) can coerce a domain controller to authenticate back to a chosen host using its machine account. Delegated TGTs can cross a two-way forest trust. In the demo, an attacker who controls a domain controller in one forest triggers the printer bug against a domain controller in the partner forest, captures that machine account's TGT from memory, imports it, and performs a DCSync against the victim forest. The demonstration used stock trust settings on patched Windows Server 2012 or later systems.

The speakers describe how Microsoft first closed the report as won't fix, then reversed the decision and issued a CVE. Mitigations discussed include selective authentication and disabling TGT delegation on each side of a trust. A patch is described that blocks cross-forest TGT delegation by default, with an opt-in flag for environments that need it. The main takeaway for practitioners is that a forest's security depends on every forest it trusts, which matters during acquisitions.

talks.title: TR19: No more dumb hex!
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for TR19: No more dumb hex!.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In "TR19: No more dumb hex!", security engineer Ange Albertini ("Ange") and front-end developer Rafał present modern alternatives to traditional hex editors and binary viewers. Conventional hex editors display fixed 16-byte wrapping with dual columns (hex and ASCII) that treat all bytes equally, losing structural context and making binary analysis and crafting cumbersome. The speakers propose two parallel approaches to address these limitations: enhancing the classic view with structured, constraint-based rendering, and replacing raw hex editing altogether using assembly language.

### Key Topics
- **Limitations of Traditional Hex Editors**: Hex views historically wrapped at 16 bytes (or 8 bytes on 40-column systems like the Apple II) simply because of 80-column terminal defaults. They separate parsers from views, display compressed data and null blocks verbatim, and fail to highlight boundaries between logical fields.
- **Grammar Parsers and Kaitai Struct**: While tools like Kaitai Struct provide excellent declarative YAML grammars and format parsing, traditional tree-plus-hex visual layouts remain rigid and difficult to navigate horizontally and vertically, lacking built-in editing capabilities.
- **The 'bud' Architecture ('this' and 'that')**: A modular framework separating file parsing from rendering via lightweight JSON representations. `this` acts as an instrumentation/parser module outputting minimal field boundaries and values, while `that` consists of renderers including a Python terminal ANSI output tool (`that.py`) and a JavaScript-based SVG renderer (`that.js`).
- **Albert & Constraint-Based Layouts**: Using the Cassowary constraint solving algorithm, Rafał created Albert—a standalone, client-side JavaScript low-level SVG builder with only one dependency. Albert translates layout relationships (margins, equal widths, relative alignments) into mathematically solved SVG diagrams and themes (e.g., Solarized, Dracula) without font-dependence breakage.
- **Binary Crafting via NASM Assembly**: Replacing hex editing entirely by using NASM as a data preprocessor (`DB`, `DW`, `DD`, macro calculations, and `incbin`). This approach treats binaries as modular text sources, simplifying file format dissection, offset recalculations, and the generation of complex polyglots and hash collisions.

### Technical Details
- **Constraint Solving**: Cassowary defines mathematical relationships between element properties ($X, Y, \text{width}, \text{height}$). Setting constraints like fixed 20-pixel spacing or aligned centers avoids hardcoding positions across disparate file sizes, though debugging can present unexpected solver behavior when element dimensions scale inversely.
- **Assembly Representation**: Rather than writing instruction mnemonics, NASM is used strictly for byte definition. Large uninspected blobs are included via `incbin`, while relevant headers, endianness macros, and offsets (`$` notation for relative line addresses) are explicitly named. Comments replace unnecessary labels to avoid polluting namespaces, allowing post-processors to compute CRCs and hashes dynamically.
- **File Crafting & Polyglots**: Ange demonstrated how structural assembly macros allowed crafting complex polyglot files (e.g., combining JAR, ZIP, and PDF/HTML), where blocks of assembly can be repositioned and automatically recalculated.

### Takeaways
Separating the parsing layer (`this`) from rendering (`that` and `Albert`) produces reusable, vector-based, and copy-pasteable visual artifacts suitable for technical papers and slides without losing structural fidelity. For advanced binary manipulation and polyglot research, declaring structures via an assembler like NASM offers significant advantages over manual byte editing.

talks.title: TR19: Abusing privileged file operations on Windows
talks.teaser: Walks concrete Windows escalation paths that abuse junctions, oplocks, rotations, and antivirus privileged file copies.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames privilege file operation bugs as stable logic flaws: privileged processes perform ordinary file actions on paths an unprivileged user can influence, without memory corruption. The speaker argues these issues are approachable with process monitors, ACL checks, and public redirection techniques from prior research, including toolkit support when built-in tools fall short.

Core exploitation chains combine NTFS junctions with object-manager symbolic links to steer creates, writes, and DLL loads. A recurring pattern ties permissive log-file ACLs, writable ProgramData-style locations, and privileged writers to drop payloads under system directories and trigger service loads. When inherited permissions block in-place overwrite, rotation and rename operations become primitives to place attacker-chosen content. Oplocks time races; bait-and-switch updates symlinks mid-access. Antivirus scanning adds high-privilege file copies, renames, and deletions that the talk walks through as concrete escalation paths, alongside generic deletion-to-recreate tricks in user-writable caches.

Recent product findings are cited, with notes that patch status can disagree with vendor advisories. Defenders are advised to keep privileged code off user-controlled paths, use impersonation or restricted tokens, and watch for junctions, oplocks, and unusual drop patterns. A brief Q&A contrasts DLL proxying risks with one-shot service hijacks for persistent offensive use.

The speaker begins with a device that came with little documentation, so the work starts with the circuit board itself: locating connectors, reading datasheets and finding test points that expose a serial debug interface. From there, the protocol the module uses is reverse engineered.

The middle of the talk follows the investigation. By reaching the chip's debug interface, the speaker gets the device into a bootloader mode and reads its firmware out. Traffic analysis shows how the module connects to its servers and how an over-the-air update is triggered by a message the server sends. Within the firmware, the speaker points to a format string issue in code that handles input, and explains how memory addresses were located so they could be used. The demonstration sends requests to the module and shows a file transfer.

For a practitioner, the main takeaway is that aftermarket car connectivity hardware can expose remote control paths that were never meant to be reachable, and that update mechanisms need the same scrutiny as the rest of the firmware. The talk shows that reverse engineering such a device is practical with standard hardware debugging and firmware analysis, even without vendor documentation.

Ryan and Travis revisit anti-emulation tricks from PoC||GTFO and earlier x86 work, this time targeting MIPS branch delay slots and MIPS16 prefix words. They explain how delayed instructions after returns can legally touch the return register on real silicon while emulators often treat prefix-extended delay-slot encodings differently.

Their experiments with QEMU show that illegal extended no-ops fault, yet a crafted extend-plus-add sequence makes QEMU increment a return value where hardware leaves it unchanged, yielding a six-byte oracle between emulation and metal. They port the idea into shellcode that prints different banners, demo the split on a remote MIPS shell account versus QEMU, and note that disassemblers such as IDA hide opcode bytes and therefore agree with the emulator.

The speakers suggest peppering delay slots across firmware to frustrate analysis, cite their PoC||GTFO write-ups, and field questions on mixed ARM/Thumb polyglots.

talks.title: TR18/NGI18: IPv6 Address Management - The First Five Years
talks.teaser: It distills five years of enterprise IPv6 allocation, flexible segment planning, and workable IPAM workflows.
talks.summary:
The session opens with how mid-sized and large organizations typically become local Internet registries and receive IPv6 blocks, including how strict filtering and out-of-region route announcements behaved in practice versus older guidance. The speaker contrasts prescriptive address governance with a descriptive, inventory-oriented view, then walks through seven objectives planners often weight—persistence, applicability, scalability, aggregation, delegation, and human-readable numbering—and argues several are routinely overvalued in fast-moving enterprises.

A large-customer case study pits a textbook site-and-service scheme against handing each organizational entity its own chunk with local autonomy. The recommended model keeps a /32 on nibble boundaries, assigns sequential segment identifiers as delegable /44 blocks, optionally uses a sub-ID nibble for non-routable or filtered space, and leaves lower-level structure to each team. The closing section stresses operational process over perfect diagrams: requesters, address admins, ticketing, IPAM integration, optional automation for non-routable assignments, and RIPE object updates when space must appear on the global Internet.

Practitioners should treat IPv6 global space unlike RFC 1918 IPv4, plan to avoid painful renumbering, and invest early in distribution workflow because deployment now rides on short cloud, data-center, and transformation projects rather than multi-year greenfield designs.

Gabriela Bentele compares IPv6 readiness across Alibaba, AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure after a customer asked whether data-center address plans could extend cleanly into IaaS VPCs. Only AWS offers native dual-stack VPCs with delegated /56 prefixes, slow reverse-DNS workflows, and no VPN-over-v6; rivals rely on NAT64 or load-balancer front-ends that hide client addresses and complicate compliance logging for mail or audits.

Live demos show Google forwarding headers preserving original IPv6 while backends remain IPv4-only, and Azure requiring fragile CLI steps before GUI configuration. She questions whether enterprises should adopt IaaS for generic servers versus buying SaaS, warns IPv6 cloud projects often restart addressing from scratch, and notes Hurricane Electric tunnels are a poor substitute for provider-native dual stack at data-center scale.

A South American researcher extends IPv6 reconnaissance by chaining search-engine scraping, NS and MX harvesting, address6 prefix extraction, and DNS reverse walks into one iterative tool nicknamed Pipita. Bing and Startpage queries bypass some anti-bot hurdles that block curl, while rate limits on Startpage curb zone-wide harvesting.

The workflow loops domains to addresses to slash-48 prefixes and back through reverse DNS until convergence, with filters to keep scope on a target organization's zones. Supporting address6 tweaks add fixed-length textual IPv6 forms for script-friendly analytics, aiming to automate pen-test recon that previously required juggling multiple CLI utilities.

talks.title: TR18/NGI18: Knockin' on IPv6's doors
talks.teaser: Demonstrates IPv6 enumeration tools, public DNS data sources, and measurements for mapping servers, routers, and prefixes at scale.
talks.summary:
The session continues practical work on knocking on IPv6’s doors: normalizing addresses for scripting, deriving slash-48 prefixes for reverse DNS, and chaining small utilities into a loop that harvests domain names, DNS records, and IPv6 services from hints with optional zone filters. Live demos cover search-engine crawlers, batching by top-level domain and country suffix, and why unfocused runs pull in unrelated zones.

The speaker describes building a broad IPv6-oriented dataset using popularity lists, voluntary zone-file programs, registries that publish zone data, and long-running crawls for sectors like military TLDs. Follow-on measurement compares interface-ID patterns on popular domains before and after privacy-oriented RFC guidance, finding more random identifiers while predictable and MAC-embedded forms remain common on public servers. Traceroute from several global vantage points maps routers; peering exchange and probe measurement APIs add high-value router and customer-prefix leads.

Operational lessons include filtering noisy reverse-DNS wildcard spaces, preferring longer prefixes when coarser reverse walks fail, and treating leaked internal-looking PTR names and still-open zone transfers as real exposure. Audience questions contrast how completely IPv6 server space can be enumerated versus opaque client prefixes, and note home CPE may be harder to spot unless probe or ISP data reveals patterns.

talks.title: TR18: I forgot Your password
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for TR18: I forgot Your password.
talks.summary:
## Overview

Noel Sanchez and Marta Morena present research on critical vulnerabilities discovered in SAP HANA's User Self-Service (USS) application, the default platform for password recovery and account creation. USS is a web application built on SAP HANA's development platform using XSJS (server-side JavaScript) that authenticates to the database using a privileged technical user with account creation and password modification capabilities.

## Key Topics

### Common Password Recovery Patterns
The speakers explain why password recovery mechanisms are high-value attack targets: nearly every modern system implements them, no secure default solution exists, the code is often developed by junior developers, and recovery functions perform critical unauthenticated actions. Common implementations include plain-text storage, random password resets, email-based reset tokens, and security questions.

### Vulnerabilities Discovered

**1. User Enumeration** - Attackers can enumerate valid usernames through differing error messages during password reset requests.

**2. Email Header Injection** - The HTTP Host header used in email templates is not sanitized and controlled by attackers, enabling phishing attacks against administrators.

**3. Blacklist Bypass** - IP blacklist checks against the X-Forwarded-For header can be bypassed by appending approximately 1,067 garbage characters, filling the array and preventing address matching.

**4. Token-Security Answer Confusion** - The most critical vulnerability stems from storing both password reset tokens and security answers in the same database table without differentiation. Security answers are not validated for format, allowing attackers to inject JSON payloads. The key format (USERNAME.security_underscore_answer) is predictable.

**5. SQL Injection via JSON Injection** - Usernames are concatenated into SQL queries without prepared statements. Although usernames are validated at creation, the application retrieves usernames from database JSON values. Attackers can inject usernames containing SQL comments and special characters through the security answer mechanism to execute arbitrary SQL, including activating the deactivated system user.

## Technical Attack Chain

The researchers demonstrate a multi-step account takeover exploiting token-security answer confusion and SQL injection:

1. Register a test account and intercept the validation request
2. Inject a JSON payload into the security answer field containing SQL injection code that activates the system user via ALTER USER system ACTIVATE statement
3. Request a new password reset token
4. Inject another JSON payload with the target victim's username to hijack their account
5. Use the hijacked account token to set a new password for any user, including the system user
6. Login as the system user

The system user is SAP HANA's most privileged account—created by default, capable of granting itself any roles, reading/modifying all database records, and modifying application source code. Obtaining system user access enables complete platform compromise.

## Takeaways

The researchers conclude that password recovery mechanism complexity is the root cause, with many implementations combining multiple methods insecurely. Recovery features should be treated with the same security rigor as authentication mechanisms. The primary remediation is using prepared statements instead of query concatenation. SAP released security notes addressing these vulnerabilities; affected versions span SPS 9 through SPS 12. Mitigations include applying patches, disabling USS if unused, and restricting access to trusted hosts.

talks.title: TR18: Hunting crypto secrets in SAP systems
talks.teaser: Covers CommonCryptoLib PSE and PCA placement, SSO pin unlock paths, and offline versus on-host decryption needs for attackers.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames a gap many SAP deployments share: wide use of encryption without equal attention to where keys, certificates, and pins actually live. It follows last year's crypto-layer work and deliberately avoids new CVEs or live exploits, aiming instead to explain mechanisms well enough to secure or test them.

Most attention goes to CommonCryptoLib's Personal Security Environment and the PCA container format used for certificates and keys across NetWeaver ABAP, file system and database stores, and HANA's in-database PSE storage. The speaker walks through PIN-based protection, PKCS-style encryption and iteration changes after 2017, SSO credential files that hold decryption pins for unattended startup, Windows DPAPI and Linux TPM paths via the local protection store, and how fallback modes still lean on hard-coded library material.

Two attacker stories tie the pieces together: stolen PSE files with PIN cracking when LPS is absent, versus combined PSE and SSO access with offline decryption or domain backup keys on Windows. Impact spans database ciphertext, forged digital signatures in business workflows, and TLS or SNC impersonation. Closing guidance favors inventory, distribution awareness, strong pins, LPS on critical hosts, current library settings, and re-encryption with stronger algorithms; related tooling for reading, decrypting, and cracking PSE files is mentioned for release.

talks.title: TR18: SAP BUGS: The Phantom Security
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding TR18: SAP BUGS: The Phantom Security.
talks.summary:
## Overview

Vihan and Vladimir from Earpiece present critical security vulnerabilities discovered in SAP systems, demonstrating an exploitation chain from directory traversal to remote code execution through Redwood and CRM components.

## Key Topics

**SAP Security Context**: SAP releases approximately 300 security patches annually. In 2017 alone, 313 critical vulnerabilities were patched. The SAP Java stack comprises thousands of applications deployed across enterprise systems.

**Redwood Component Directory Traversal (2016)**: The Redwood scheduler servlet contains a directory traversal vulnerability in the UIUtil JavaScript servlet. By manipulating the "util" parameter with traversal sequences (../), attackers can read arbitrary files without authentication. This allows access to critical secure storage files containing administrator credentials and database connection strings.

**Secure Storage Decryption**: SAP servers store sensitive data in encrypted files (sexstore.properties and sexstore.key). The speakers developed a "sexstore decrypter" tool exploiting the encryption implementation. The encryption uses Triple DES in CBC mode with a hard-coded key found in Java source code. By decrypting these files, attackers obtain plain-text administrator passwords and database credentials.

**CRM Component RCE Chain**: A second directory traversal vulnerability in SAP CRM service enables: (1) changing log file location and extension, (2) redirecting logs to application directories, (3) modifying extension to .JSP, (4) writing JSP shellcode via malformed requests, (5) executing arbitrary Java code when SAP parses the JSP files. The speakers automated this via Python scripts sending specially crafted requests containing JSP code within error messages.

**Practical Impact**: Approximately 500 publicly accessible SAP servers with Redwood component were discovered on the internet. The combined vulnerabilities enable unauthenticated attackers to gain full administrative access and execute arbitrary commands.

**Remediation**: Install SAP security patches for Redwood and CRM, apply firewall rules restricting CRM connections, and install additional security notes from SAP/NIST.

The speakers demonstrated live exploitation showing file reading, credential decryption, and command execution on compromised SAP systems.

talks.title: TR18: Active Directory Security: The Journey
talks.teaser: Traces Active Directory security from Windows 2000 onward, covering Kerberos delegation risks, admin tiering and hardening advice.
talks.summary:
Sean Metcalf walks through the history of Active Directory security, from design decisions made for Windows 2000 that still shape many environments to the protections added in later Windows releases. He sorts the current state into what is improving, such as wider use of local admin password management and PowerShell 5 adoption, and what remains weak, including domain admins logging into ordinary workstations, legacy password-length requirements, and gaps in domain controller logging.

The middle of the talk focuses on privilege paths. He shows how Exchange's built-in groups hold broad rights over directory objects that scans of ordinary permissions can miss, and how the password sync account used by Azure AD Connect can expose password data through replication-style requests. He also explains how unconstrained, constrained and protocol-transition Kerberos delegation let an attacker impersonate users once a trusted server is compromised, and covers risky default domain controller policy settings, group policy reuse that pushes server admins into domain admin groups, and an RDP session hijack on an admin server.

For defenders, he recommends marking admin accounts as sensitive and not delegatable or placing them in the Protected Users group, logging the Kerberos and logon events that reveal password spraying and offline ticket cracking, and starting a tiered administration model by protecting tier zero first. He presents Microsoft's red forest approach as the most secure option while noting its cost and limits.

talks.title: TR18: Attack and defend Microsoft Enhanced Security Administrative Environment
talks.teaser: Shows how attackers move from tier 1 and tier 2 access to domain controllers in a Microsoft red forest environment.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, penetration testers Hao and Pipe discuss techniques for attacking and hardening Microsoft's Enhanced Security Administrative Environment (ESAE), commonly known as a Red Forest. While the ESAE tiered administrative model (Tier 0, Tier 1, and Tier 2) is designed to isolate administrative credentials and prevent lateral movement from standard workstations or servers into domain controllers, real-world misconfigurations and secondary management channels often allow attackers to bypass these boundaries and escalate privileges to Tier 0.

### Key Topics
The speakers outline several major vectors used to bridge tiers:
- Abusing Active Directory permissions and discovering overlooked "shadow admin" accounts.
- Subverting virtualization infrastructure (such as VMware vSphere) hosting virtualized domain controllers.
- Abusing centralized endpoint security and management platforms (antivirus, configuration management, backup, and EDR tools).
- Identifying weaknesses and misconfigurations in Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) provisioning and self-service portals.

### Technical Details
- **Active Directory Permission Abuse & Shadow Admins**: Attackers search for accounts with non-standard administrative privileges such as `Replicating Directory Changes` and `Replicating Directory Changes All` (enabling DCSync attacks). Service accounts in applications like Microsoft SharePoint (User Profile Service account), Riverbed SteelHead, and on-premises directory synchronization servers frequently hold these permissions. Additionally, Microsoft Exchange servers (via `Exchange Windows Permissions` and `Exchange Trusted Subsystem`) possess domain-wide write rights; running as `NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM` on an Exchange server allows granting DCSync rights to standard users using tools like PowerView. Attackers can also target write permissions on the `AdminSDHolder` container, which propagates permissions to protected groups.
- **Virtualization Infrastructure Attacks**: Virtual domain controllers expose Tier 0 to hypervisor administrators. Attackers leveraging compromised vCenter credentials or console access can bypass network segmentation. By using data store browsers, PowerCLI scripts, or tools like Veeam Backup to take snapshots, attackers can extract raw VMDK files. Once downloaded, multi-part VMDKs can be merged, loopback-mounted on Linux, or parsed with forensic tools to extract `NTDS.dit` hashes without ever directly touching the running OS (provided full-disk encryption is not implemented).
- **Endpoint Management Exploitation**: Centralized agents running as `NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM` cross tier boundaries. In Symantec Endpoint Protection, an attacker with console access can configure Host Integrity policies using VBScript payloads to create a user and add them to Domain Admins on managed domain controllers. Similarly, Microsoft SCCM (via GUI or PowerSCCM), Veritas NetBackup (restoring `ntds.dit` from unencrypted backups), and cloud-hosted EDR platforms (like Carbon Black, targeted via phishing and live-response shells) can be weaponized for code execution and credential harvesting.
- **MFA Provisioning Weaknesses**: Attackers exploit self-service portals that rely solely on single-factor domain credentials or default ports (e.g., port 7004). Flaws include unexpired enrollment links left in mailboxes, unmonitored enrollment that lacks notifications, missing rate limits on registered devices, look-up table PDF cards stored in inboxes, and reusable QR activation codes.

### Takeaways
To properly defend ESAE and Active Directory environments:
- Audit permissions for shadow admin rights, not just explicit group memberships, treating accounts with DCSync or object modification rights as Tier 0.
- Strictly isolate virtualization infrastructure hosting domain controllers, or keep Tier 0 on dedicated hardware, and mandate full disk encryption for virtual DCs.
- Implement separate, segmented endpoint security and management infrastructure per tier so management agents cannot bridge Tier 1/2 to Tier 0.
- Secure MFA provisioning by expiring enrollment links, requiring multi-factor authentication to access self-service consoles, and enforcing device enrollment limits and notifications.
- Restrict and rotate credentials using Managed Service Accounts (gMSAs) and dedicated privileged access workstations.

talks.title: TR18: Mind the Gap, Bro
talks.teaser: Open-source network monitors at choke points carve transit files and run pattern checks where industrial hosts lack centralized logging.
talks.summary:
The speaker argues that strong security visibility needs both host and network telemetry, but many industrial and legacy environments lack mature endpoint logging while switches and TAPs still offer controlled capture points. The core idea is to treat strategic network choke points as places to recover host-like artifacts—files, scripts, and protocol behavior—while adversaries move staging data across segmented IT and control networks.

The walkthrough centers on Bro (Zeek) for protocol-aware file carving from SMB, HTTP, FTP, and similar traffic, then pairing extracted objects with Yara and light unpacking scripts rather than treating Yara solely as antivirus. Case studies include Crash Override staging over SMB and living-off-the-land tooling, TRISIS movement of compiled Python payloads toward Triconex safety controllers, and DYMALLOY-style exfiltration of HMI screenshots detected by resolution-aware image checks.

Limitations receive equal attention: widespread encryption blunts content inspection, though JA3 fingerprinting and certificate metadata sometimes still help; compound Office and archive types need unpacking pipelines; and flat or poorly segmented designs reduce midpoint visibility. The closing message is deliberately imperfect but practical—network-derived detection catches one required step in a long attack chain, enabling earlier response when full host coverage is unrealistic.

talks.title: TR18: Subverting Trust in Windows
talks.teaser: Hands-on demos show how Windows signature validation and cloned certificate chains let attackers subvert defender trust in signed code.
talks.summary:
The session is a demo-heavy walkthrough of how defenders often over-trust code signing on Windows, and how an attacker can abuse that mindset. It opens by framing “trust” for enterprise software: vendor reputation, software intent, abuse of signed utilities such as PowerShell, protection of signing keys, and whether the OS truly validates signer origin and integrity. The speaker contrasts maturity levels from blind faith and antivirus-heavy models through reputation-based application control to formal whitelisting, and stresses that signing attests origin and integrity—not safety or intent—while noting that failed integrity checks on signed code may still execute without strong user warning.

Two manual attacks are demonstrated end to end. The first hijacks the portable-executable Subject Interface Package in the registry so indirect signature verification can be redirected to a benign export that always succeeds, after crafting an embedded authenticode-style blob from catalog signature material so an unsigned sample can appear Microsoft-signed in tools such as Sigcheck once the hijack is active. The second clones the visible fields of a kernel32 certificate chain, signs a binary with a forged leaf, and trusts a cloned root in the user certificate store—sometimes without administrative rights beyond a confirmation prompt—so validation utilities report a familiar Microsoft chain until thumbprints are checked against expected roots.

Practitioners are urged not to filter out or auto-trust events merely because the publisher is Microsoft, to watch unusual paths and persistence, and to verify trust using certificate thumbprints against Microsoft’s published trusted root list rather than publisher strings alone. The talk points to a long whitepaper on SIP and trust-provider hijacking and a blog post on cloning attacks with prevention and detection guidance.

talks.title: TR18: Real-Life Network and Security Automation
talks.teaser: Surveys real-world network automation projects, from read-only data collection to fully automated site deployments.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a skeptic's question about managing many vendors and thousands of devices. The speaker answers with a staged path: start with read-only access, move on to device provisioning, and only then automate service provisioning. The material comes from about 300 people in an online course who built their own tools, often because vendor products were too expensive, lacked a needed feature, or were too heavy for a small problem.

The early examples are simple but practical. One integrator used an Ansible playbook to check device uptime after a campus power outage, instead of logging into hundreds of devices by hand. Another engineer compared expected and actual LLDP neighbours to verify a switch build-out during construction. Further cases include a half-matrix of pings to flag latency anomalies, parsing Nexus transceiver output to plan optics replacements, and exporting Cisco ACI data into spreadsheets. Later projects generate topology graphs for VLANs and IP multicast from device output, enforce consistent firewall settings, and handle zero-touch provisioning keyed on MAC addresses. A telco deploys MPLS customer sites in about ten minutes, and a government body refreshed nearly 2,000 sites using spreadsheet-driven templates and CDP-based topology checks. A Swiss bank rebuilt 24 data centers from identical templates with automated tests.

The speaker notes that multi-vendor standard data models still have gaps and that many devices lack SSH command mode. The takeaway is that network engineers need systems thinking, data models and some programming skills, that vendor demos should be treated with caution, and that building small, useful tools is a practical place to start.

The duo contrasts immutable infrastructure cheerleading with practical CI/CD risks: poisoned build scripts, registry overrides, missing enforcement between build and production, and container scanners that miss app-layer dependencies. They argue security must insert a gated promotion service rather than handing every developer root-equivalent build power. Rolling deployments, canary metrics, and zoning build hosts appear as mitigations once attendees see the live sock-puppet deploy fail its demo moment.

talks.title: TR18: Ads networks are following you, follow them back
talks.teaser: A toolkit turns ad-network HTTP archives into domain trees so investigators can map third-party tracking on news sites.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with why major news sites depend on ad and third-party scripts, and why media lawyers lack practical ways to audit hundreds of domains and requests on a single homepage. Phishing investigations share the same pain: dynamic JavaScript, user-agent branching, and environments that differ from reporters’ locked-down browsers make cases hard to reproduce and document.

The core approach loads a URL through Splash in Docker, captures a full HTTP archive with headers, cookies, bodies, and screenshots, then builds a request tree from Location and Referer links, iframe relationships, and regex URL extraction from response bodies. Results aggregate by domain using ETE Toolkit, exposed as a Python library and a collapsible web UI where analysts can inspect nodes, download payloads, and spot untethered URLs that imply hidden dynamic loads.

Live demos on bloomberg.com, theguardian.com, and stallman.org illustrate shallow versus deep ad graphs, tracking pixels, and multi-level redirect chains. The speaker positions the stack as open source, aimed eventually at less technical stakeholders, with planned features such as user-agent comparison, cookie lineage views, block lists in Splash, and hashes to flag altered JavaScript libraries. Practitioners gain a repeatable pipeline from one page load to a shareable map of who loads whom.

talks.title: TR18: The Wolf In SGX Clothing
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of TR18: The Wolf In SGX Clothing.

Intel researcher Marion Masek explores whether ransomware and other malware can live inside Intel SGX enclaves, reprising industry panic that antivirus cannot see enclave memory. She differentiates on-disk binaries—which remain signature-able—from runtime DRAM that debuggers and endpoint tools struggle to inspect once code runs inside an enclave.

Demos copy shellcode into enclave-readable sections, proxy syscalls from enclave to host libc, and discuss read-write-execute staging on Linux. She argues protections help confidentiality yet complicate incident response, notes most enclave code is SDK boilerplate, and invites debate on whether memory introspection or attestation policies are the realistic detection pivot.

talks.title: TR18: When Virtual Hell Freezes Over
talks.teaser: An IDA Python workflow rebuilds MSVC C++ vtables so reversers can tie virtual calls to named functions without endless manual tracing.
talks.summary:
Cal frames reversing Microsoft Visual C++ binaries as painstaking framework work before application logic: dynamic allocation, constructors, single and multiple inheritance, and especially vtables make virtual calls opaque in disassembly because only register loads and indirect calls remain visible. The talk walks inheritance examples showing how vtable layouts differ when derived classes override or add virtual methods, and why multiple inheritance forces non-virtual calls that name a base while other dispatches stay unknown until runtime.

To reduce that grind, Cal describes a personal IDA tool chain built with Python and, where needed, IDC. Tracing breakpoints were rejected as too manual and narrow. Instead the approach scans for virtual calls, places software breakpoints on vtable pointer setup, and uses always-false conditional breakpoints so hook scripts run without halting execution. A notable hurdle was that IDA exposes rich Python helpers only when breakpoint conditions are marked Python, which required manually adjusting breakpoint language via the API. Hooks capture vtable bases and resolved slots, rebuild function lists, define vtable structures in the database, annotate structures and disassembly with cross-references, and replace raw offsets with readable function names tied to researcher renames or symbols already present.

Live before-and-after slides show yellow-marked virtual calls transforming into documented vtables, comments, and correlated call sites for multiple-inheritance samples. Scope today is x86 MSVC; other compilers and architectures are future work, as is automatic object layout recovery and richer naming from strings or callees. Practitioners gain a repeatable pattern for automating vtable discovery and keeping assembly, structures, and comments aligned while reversing C++.

talks.title: TR18: Robots Panel
talks.teaser: A panel weighs robot ownership, ethics, privacy, liability, and safety as machines blend physical action with sensors and AI.
talks.summary:
The session opens by aligning on what counts as a robot—sensors, actuators, intelligence, and a physical body—and whether ownership belongs in that picture. Panelists contrast industrial arms with social machines, touching on repair rights, companionship after an owner dies, and how design and language around “owning” robots echo harmful human biases.

Discussion moves through harm and deception: vandalism on expensive street units versus abuse of emotionally expressive social robots, white lies in elder care or search-and-rescue, and who should set ethics when vendors bake in gendered or nonfunctional traits. Privacy expectations, NDAs, and recorded telemetry follow, along with liability when behavior is opaque, insurance models, worker displacement, and half-serious questions about taxes and votes.

The close covers retirement rituals, factory resets, emotional bonds, decades-long industrial deployments, and vendor security response. Panelists argue for early security and safety in design, realistic user expectations, and treating physical robots as more than ordinary computers.

talks.title: TR18: Reverse Engineering Black Box Systems with GreatFET
talks.teaser: Shows how USB proxies and device emulation can probe closed embedded systems such as consoles and TVs.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how USB can be used to probe black box systems such as games consoles, cars, TVs and projectors when their software cannot be inspected. The speakers point out that hosts trust attached USB devices, and that embedded hosts are hard to virtualise the way a desktop driver can be. They introduce USB proxy tooling and the open source GreatFET platform, with FaceDancer for device emulation, to sit between a device and its host.

A live demo routed a game controller through the board into a Nintendo console, where a two-line Python change to a HID descriptor flipped the joystick axis. Emulating a flash drive showed that the order of enumeration and the reads a host makes can reveal its operating system or USB stack version. A fake file allocation table can also expose which filenames a host looks for, using timing differences to narrow them down character by character. In one firmware update example, a device read its image twice, checking the first copy and flashing the second, so swapping the file between reads loaded attacker data.

Glitching with the GlitchKit framework, which uses USB events for timing fault injection, was described as a route to dumping firmware from embedded devices. Practitioners should treat USB as a real attack surface on closed systems, and firmware updates that re-read data are worth checking for time-of-check gaps.

talks.teaser: Examines dealer infrastructure, VCI devices, and UDS protocols as a scalable path to compromise non-connected vehicles.
talks.summary:
The presenters describe automotive security research from an Israeli team that cannot name their vehicle vendor while discussions with the manufacturer continue. They outline why car security differs from mainstream IT: sparse public incident data, costly recall-driven patching, and vehicles that remain on the road with decade-old embedded software. Familiar entry points such as OBD ports, infotainment stacks, and telematics attracted prior high-profile work, yet the vast majority of vehicles lack always-on connectivity.

Their focus shifts to OEM repair ecosystems. Certified shops connect vehicles through vehicle communication interfaces that bridge diagnostics, firmware delivery, and sometimes cloud backends. The talk maps theoretical and partially tested attack surfaces across OEM clouds, outdated shop PCs, internet-exposed VCIs, and malicious vehicles that subvert the interface when technicians connect them. Compromising a VCI places an attacker between the car, technician workstation, and update pipeline with blast radius beyond a single bay.

The closing segment explains Controller Area Network messaging and uses compromised VCI code execution to intercept or replay UDS programming sessions, including manufacturer seed-and-key unlock flows recovered through static reverse engineering of two VCI generations. Practitioners should treat workshop infrastructure as part of the vehicle threat model, respect physical safety constraints, and pursue vendor cooperation before experimentation.

talks.title: Cloud Seeding
talks.teaser: Shows how a ride-hailing app's sign-up and SMS verification can be abused at scale to create accounts and take free rides.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how a ride-hailing service's mobile app and cloud API can be used in ways their designers did not intend. The researchers decompiled the Android app, found leftover test code and embedded keys, and got past certificate pinning by pulling the key store password, adding their own certificate and re-signing the app so its traffic could be proxied. The API then revealed that nearby drivers could be queried across a city grid, and that sign-up checks were light, with real verification only when a ride was requested.

The main experiment was automated account creation. The team used a telephony API to buy cheap numbers for verification texts, scripted sign-ups with randomized details, and used promo and referral codes to get free rides. They also showed that the verification request could be triggered for any known user ID, and that a four-digit PIN could be brute forced across many unverified accounts, with two accounts verified in about a minute. A second app was shown to reuse shared phone numbers, letting a tester log into existing accounts.

The speakers also outlined possible impacts, such as flooding demand to drain driver supply, and argued that phone numbers are a weak basis for identity and that backends should not trust the client. They said they had not reported the issues to the vendors, viewing them as design choices rather than bugs.

talks.teaser: Reverse engineers TP-Link smart plug and camera protocols, uncovering weak obfuscation, missing authentication and packet loop abuse.
talks.summary:
The talk examines TP-Link smart plugs and IP cameras from the protocol level. The speaker explains that the plugs use a JSON-based protocol on port 9999, carried over UDP or TCP. The TCP variant adds a four-byte length field before the payload. The payload is only lightly obfuscated with a well-known key, so anyone sniffing the local network can read the commands. Discovery uses a broadcast query that returns device details and, on metered models, power readings.

The speaker then covers the weaknesses found. The protocol has no authentication, so anyone with local access can control a device, and UDP packets can be spoofed. Repeated fields can inflate packet size, and two devices can be made to answer each other's error responses in a loop until the network drops the traffic. A helper tool toggles a relay every 50 milliseconds for a set duration. The TDDP protocol derives its key from an MD5 digest of the username and password, which are often left at defaults, and it has no replay protection. Camera streams are reachable over HTTP with the camera credentials.

The closing section looks ahead to IPv6. Services built for the local network could become globally reachable once devices gain IPv6 addresses, so the speaker recommends border firewalls and a pull-based device model. Controlling devices locally, rather than through the vendor cloud, is also suggested. The tools are in a Git repository, and a write-up is planned.

talks.teaser: Walks through application whitelisting bypasses against Device Guard, with an MSBuild demo, and the mitigations defenders can apply.
talks.summary:
This talk looks at application allowlisting with Microsoft's Device Guard from both the offensive and defensive side, arguing that testing these controls makes defenders better. The speakers separate naive attackers, who drop and run binaries without knowing the defenses, from enlightened attackers who study and bypass them. They argue allowlisting removes most of the naive class and forces enlightened attackers to change their tradecraft.

The bypasses are grouped into policy misconfiguration, misplaced trust, constrained language mode weaknesses, vulnerable trusted drivers and implementation flaws. For policy, they show how a rule that trusts a certificate issuer, rather than a specific publisher, is far too broad, and how policy drift gradually widens permissions over time. For misplaced trust, they demonstrate MSBuild compiling inline C# from an XML project file and loading a credential-dumping tool in memory on a Device Guard system, where the same binary is blocked on disk. For PowerShell, a trusted script calling Add-Type can be steered to run unsigned code in full language mode. Each category is paired with its mitigation and the party that owns it, such as the administrator, Microsoft or third-party vendors.

The practical advice is to start in audit mode with a deny-by-default policy, begin with drivers and fixed-function machines, enforce minimum versions for vulnerable drivers, block tools like MSBuild where they are not needed, and treat every trusted signer as an explicit decision.
