talks.title: TROOPERS14 - Risks in hosted SAP Environments
talks.teaser: Shows how hosted SAP landscapes can be breached through a central Solution Manager or cross-client access on shared systems.
talks.summary:
The talk examines the security risks for customers whose SAP systems run in a hosted environment. The presenters open with a public incident involving a UK police hosting arrangement, then describe two hosting models: many customers' systems maintained from one central Solution Manager, and several companies sharing a single SAP system separated by client. In the first model, Solution Manager keeps stored RFC connection credentials for every hosted system, so compromising it, or abusing its broad rights, can reach the whole environment. A demo showed a function module that deletes files on a connected system once the caller is authorized, and exposed Solution Manager web applications were located through a simple internet search.

For the shared-system model, client separation is enforced automatically for Open SQL, but explicit client specification, native SQL and the database connectivity interface bypass it. The presenters described two generic cross-client remote functions and ran a live attack from one client that read another client's data and reset the password of a CIO user. A survey of almost 200 custom code installations found an average of 76 cross-client accesses per standard customer installation. Two SAP advisories were reviewed: a cross-client read issue rated CVSS 3.5 and a write issue rated 6.0, with patch times of 451 and 415 days.

The takeaways are to keep Solution Manager off the internet, restrict its RFC users to the minimum needed, install SAP security notes promptly, and ask hosting providers how they handle custom code, connections and penetration testing. The presenters noted that least-privilege settings for Solution Manager are difficult to achieve in practice.

talks.title: TROOPERS14 - SAP's Network Protocols Revisited
talks.teaser: Walks through SAP network services like the router, gateway, dispatcher and message server, showing attacks and hardening advice.
talks.summary:
This talk takes a network penetration testing approach to SAP environments, focusing on the protocols behind the core NetWeaver components rather than the application layer. The speaker works black box, learning each service from network and application traces, existing research and custom tools: a Python library built on Scapy for crafting packets, and a Wireshark plugin for dissecting SAP protocols. It is presented as a review of known and newer attacks, not a step-by-step guide.

The services covered are the SAP Router, Gateway, Dispatcher, Message Server and Enqueue Server. For the router, a flaw in parsing the route string was highlighted because the packet is handled before access control checks, so an exposed router is reachable by a remote attacker. For the Gateway, monitor mode and table-formatted RFC packets were discussed, along with the risk of sniffing and rogue-server tricks against the Dispatcher's DIAG protocol. The Message Server section included a memory corruption issue, shown in a live demo where a crafted request first enabled monitor mode on a connection and a later request changed a configuration parameter.

The practical takeaways are to keep every component patched, enforce encryption, use access control lists, put the router behind a firewall, disable monitor mode when it is not needed, and separate internal and external Message Server ports. The speaker also noted newer components such as NetWeaver Gateway and SAP HANA, whose published specifications should lead to more research and attacks in the coming years.

talks.title: TROOPERS14 - OSMOSIS
talks.teaser: Shows how default installs of popular open-source monitoring tools can be chained from web flaws into shells on deep network systems.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at open-source monitoring software such as Cacti, Checkmk and OMD. These tools are widely deployed, sit deep inside networks, and have access to many servers, network devices and monitored hosts, which makes them valuable targets. The speakers reviewed mainstream tools in default configurations and focused on flaws that can be exploited in practice rather than theoretical issues. Plugins, bundled agents and the wider architecture were left out of scope.

The demonstrations used a virtualized network with an admin zone, a monitoring network, a DMZ and the internet. In Cacti, a cross-site request forgery flaw in the graph export settings let an attacker obtain a shell once a logged-in administrator opened a crafted page. A brute-force variant worked when the admin was logged out. In Checkmk, a snapshot upload feature that executes Python could be reached through a cross-site request forgery, and a cross-site scripting flaw in the agent string shown on the dashboard let an attacker use a compromised monitored host as a proxy into the monitoring network. The final chain needed only one SSH connection attempt with a crafted username, which a log-watching feature rendered in the browser. The speakers reported memory corruption, injection and remote code execution issues across the tools tested. Vendor responses varied: one fix took about six days, another about 85 days, and some vendors did not respond.

The mitigations focus on reducing exposure. Administrators should disable features they do not need, such as log watching, require key-based SSH, keep the monitoring system off the internet, and separate it from the corporate network with firewalls. Agent communication can be changed so that the central server pulls files instead of accepting direct connections. The speakers stressed that open source is not inherently more secure than commercial software, and said full details would be published after the conference.

talks.title: TROOPERS14 - Security and SDN -- A perfect fit or oil-and-water?
talks.teaser: Separates SDN hype from substance, then examines control-plane attack risks and security uses like traffic taps and DDoS blackholing.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by explaining software-defined networking. The speaker notes that the term is used loosely by vendors and startups, and that the Open Networking Foundation defines it as separating the network's control plane from its forwarding plane, so one controller manages many devices. The speaker argues that many of the underlying ideas are old, and that some, such as BGP-based remote triggered blackholing and BGP flowspec, already run in production networks.

The security section treats the controller as a high-value target, since compromising it gives an attacker control of the network, and it carries the usual risks of its operating system, language and TLS setup. Switches have a limited control-plane path, so an attacker can flood the controller with packets or force excessive flow setup. Mitigations discussed include out-of-band control networks, proactive flow installation based on known topology instead of reactive setup, distributed intelligence, and control-plane policing. The speaker warns that policing on many switches is one shared bucket, so one interface can starve the others.

The talk then covers defensive uses. Flow-based counters can measure specific traffic, flow rules can steer mirrored traffic to tap aggregation and IDS appliances, and traffic can be split across sensors by address range. In one example, an intrusion detection system asks the controller to drop a suspicious flow. The closing message is that the field is immature and changing, so practitioners should judge whether it fits their network rather than ignore it.

talks.title: TROOPERS14 - The Three Billion Dollar App
talks.teaser: Shows how an attacker reverse engineered the Android apps of Snapchat and Wickr to expose flaws in their client-side cryptography.
talks.summary:
The talk examines two mobile messaging apps, Snapchat and Wickr, which promote self-destructing or highly secure messaging, and asks whether their privacy claims and reported valuations hold up. The speaker treats the attacker as the owner of the client, so the work focuses on the Android app itself: extracting it, decompiling it, and rebuilding a custom client.

In Snapchat, request tokens were generated from client-side timestamps and static strings, so requests could be forged and replayed, and message encryption used a static key in ECB mode. Sessions never expired. A find-friends function was abused to map phone number ranges, exposing about 4.6 million usernames. An unauthenticated retry request let messages reach any user, including the sender. Snapchat fixed this within an hour after the issue was raised publicly. Wickr randomized its ciphertext and had no obvious hardcoded secrets, so the speaker turned to its native library, patched the ARM binary to expose the key and initialisation vector, and used them to decrypt and send messages. The key was reported through a bug bounty and accepted.

The main takeaway is that client-side checks such as lockouts offer little protection once an attacker controls the app, and that static keys or predictable IVs undermine encryption wherever they are embedded.

talks.title: TROOPERS14 - Making (and Breaking) an 802.15.4 WIDS
talks.teaser: Explores Zigbee radio-layer attacks and presents an open framework for sniffing, injecting and detecting them.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from Zigbee's spread into homes, buildings and industrial sites, and argues that its attack surface cannot improve until practitioners can inspect and inject traffic at the lowest layers. The speakers show that what a radio reports as a frame is really a stream of bits that the chip matches against a sync value, so whoever controls those bits can shape what receivers see. To work at that level they built a custom sniffer and injector board with an external antenna, then a Python framework called Beekeeper WIDS that splits capture, storage, analytics and alerting across a daemon, plugin-based drone hardware and a REST API.

The demonstrations cover three detections. The first targets AES-CTR replay protection: a frame carrying the maximum frame counter value causes later legitimate frames to be discarded. The second detects beacon request floods that leak network information for reconnaissance. The third detects floods of disassociation frames used to knock devices off a network. Each case is shown as a capture, a stored record and an alert raised by an analytics module.

The final section, presented by Ryan Speers, introduces the Isotope framework, which alters preamble and sync content to find transmissions that one receiver accepts while another rejects them, a fingerprinting approach that exposes differences between radio chips. The speakers say the hardware and code were released as open source. The takeaway is that defenders need the same low-level tooling attackers use, and that detection logic must match how the target radios actually parse frames.

talks.title: TROOPERS14 - Keynote
talks.teaser: Argues that hacking and security choices are political, covering exploit sales, surveillance, and arms control debates.
talks.summary:
The keynote challenges the common hacker stance that the community stays out of politics, arguing that choices such as whether to disclose a vulnerability or sell an exploit are already political. It treats a working exploit as a weapon, which raises questions about regulation and about who controls its use once released.

The middle of the talk surveys examples. A recalled anecdote describes a government contact asking for help with a highly secure BlackBerry setup, which later appeared in the press. The NSA's cheaper internal ThinThread system is contrasted with the costlier Trailblazer project, which the speaker links to contractor lobbying. Large platforms are criticised for profiting from personal profiles, and unencrypted mail and weak PGP adoption are called out. The talk also covers whistleblowing and an iterated prisoner's dilemma, where tit-for-tat is presented as a better strategy than betrayal. Other topics include national identification requirements for internet access, UN codes of conduct, export rules that now cover intrusion software, and the lack of product liability for software.

The closing urges hackers to engage with politicians, to share their knowledge of offensive security at hearings, and to avoid taking contracts that would make them lobbyists. Practical advice includes building recoverable components, limiting the identification data collected for authorization, and avoiding backdoors. The takeaway is that if technical experts stay out of the room, others will shape the rules.

talks.title: TROOPERS11 - OMG WTF PDF -- What you didn't know about Acrobat
talks.teaser: Shows how PDF parsing ambiguities let one file pose as several formats, and how that slips past detection.
talks.summary:
The talk gives an overview of the PDF format and Adobe Acrobat, starting with why PDF was created as a non-programmable alternative to PostScript. It describes a PDF as a flat, text-based tree of objects that can be extended with new revisions appended to the end, and it walks through Acrobat's added features over its versions, including JavaScript, launch actions, multimedia, forms and the recent sandboxing of the reader.

The core section looks at syntactic ambiguity. Stream lengths can disagree with the end-stream token, cross-reference offsets can be wrong or missing, and Acrobat falls back to a rebuild mode for broken files. The speaker shows that the header can sit after some leading data, so one file can be read as a PDF and also as a ZIP archive, a GIF or a Windows executable. A live demo runs a calculator binary that still works normally and also opens in Adobe Reader with embedded JavaScript running. The talk also covers how malicious PDFs hide JavaScript in annotation fields and leave older payload data behind in revisions.

The takeaway is that the specification leaves broken input undefined, so one file can be valid for several parsers at once and its behaviour cannot be judged from a single tool. In the speaker's tests, the antivirus products tried did not detect these tricks. Practitioners should treat PDF handling as inconsistent across readers and scanners when assessing what a file will do.

talks.title: TROOPERS11 - Do you know what's happening in your $application?
talks.teaser: Introduces PyBox, a Python framework for building custom sandboxes that hook functions inside running Windows applications.
talks.summary:
Felix Leder presents PyBox, a Python framework for building custom sandboxes and monitoring tools that attach to running Windows x86 processes. He first surveys where monitoring can sit, from user-mode debuggers and API hooks, through kernel system call tables, to hypervisor-based introspection and firmware. Each layer trades visibility against detectability, flexibility and performance.

The motivation is that many existing sandboxes have fixed monitoring features, cannot be reconfigured while running, and are closed. Malware that sleeps or busy-waits can also outlast time-limited analysis, so a sandbox should be tuned per malware family and stop early. PyBox injects a Python interpreter into the target and installs hooks that run before and after functions, with access to registers, arguments and memory searches. Demonstrations covered Internet Explorer, where the JavaScript passed to the compile function was logged, and Firefox, where a banking login's data was read before SSL encryption. A SpyEye sample was also analysed: it waited about 20 seconds, then moved its work to a child process, where the sandbox extracted candidate crypto keys. A final demo hooked Acrobat's JavaScript interpreter to see objects and methods registered during a heap spray.

The talk closes with limitations. The framework currently targets 32-bit Windows on Intel, and Linux, 64-bit and other architectures are future work. Evasion techniques were deliberately withheld, and output is a plain text log. Attendees were pointed to the open source release for feedback.

talks.title: TROOPERS11 - Owning the data center using Cisco NX-OS
talks.teaser: Shows how Cisco NX-OS data center switches can be compromised through hidden commands, root-level daemons, and memory bugs.
talks.summary:
George Hedfors walks through Cisco NX-OS, the operating system on Nexus data center switches, which is built on a Linux base. The talk opens with a short introduction to the platform and the history of the research. It started with an old denial-of-service issue that had been patched, and from it the speaker recovered core dumps and Linux files from firmware images. Protocol handling runs as daemons, many under root, so a single compromise can reach every virtual LAN on the device.

The middle section covers several findings. Hidden configuration entries do not appear in help or tab completion, and one of them lets a user escape the command line into the underlying Linux processes. A shell helper grants passwordless sudo, and a CDP daemon contains a memory bug where a 16-bit length is truncated to 8 bits for allocation while the copy uses the full value. An FTP account has a password but no login shell, and a password matching a sample from a certificate guide appears in the configuration. Some inputs reach shell command substitution through backticks, and a feature for switching virtual device contexts was described as one the vendor considers necessary.

A short demo on a virtual NX-OS image showed the backtick problem. The speaker argues that the design, with root-level services and sudo used throughout, cannot be fixed with a quick patch and needs rethinking. In the Q&A, the bugs shown were said to need local user access on the device. The takeaway is that owners of these switches should treat local access to the box as a serious risk and watch for vendor fixes.

talks.title: TROOPERS11 - Forging Canon Original Decision Data

talks.title: TROOPERS11 - Keynote Day 1
talks.teaser: Argues that trust, not control, must shape security as cloud, smartphones and outsourcing erode traditional network locality.
talks.summary:
Enno Rey opens Troopers in Heidelberg with organizational notes and an explanation of the event's purpose. He describes it as a meeting point for people from industry, academia and the research community, and notes about 150 registered attendees including speakers. He links it to his firm's view that theory should be shown in practice.

The central argument is that infosec faces heavy architectural change. Servers move to the cloud, front-end processing moves to smartphones, and networks move onto the internet, so locality and direct administrative control fade. Rey argues trust must replace control: third parties should be judged by past behaviour, disclosure and dependencies rather than audited and monitored. He cites a 1972 computer security study to show core problems persist, and advises keeping sensitive data off smartphones and blocking external USB devices and driver installs on control networks, with Stuxnet as proof that theoretical attacks happen.

He reviews recent incidents, including the early 2010 Google intrusion, the RSA breach, and a certificate authority incident tied to a compromised registration agent. He also points to the Japan earthquake, after which Cisco deferred a patch day. His lessons are to prepare for events outside risk assessment and to ask hard questions about who to trust.

talks.title: TROOPERS11 - Keynote Day 2
talks.teaser: Challenges security professionals to question their own narratives, assumptions and the wider political context of their work.
talks.summary:
Richard Thieme opens this keynote by arguing that the security field tells itself a comfortable story about its work, and that people inside it often lose sight of the larger picture. Drawing on decades of experience across religion, academia and consulting, he says that words such as security are used as if everyone understands them, when they should be examined. He describes how the internet was built for ease of use and had security added later, and how the national security apparatus grew after 2001.

To show the scale of that secret world, he cites figures about the United States: 1,271 government organizations and 1,931 private companies working on counterterrorism, homeland security and intelligence programs, and 854,000 people holding top secret clearances. He notes that analysts publish 50,000 intelligence reports a year, many too many to be read. He also criticises the vendor market, saying products rarely deliver the protection they promise, and argues that effective defense is more a business problem than a technology one. Banks and money laundering appear as examples of criminal money moving through the global financial system.

He closes by saying that the enemy is partly the way the field talks about itself. His practical advice is to notice when you jump to conclusions, question beliefs you no longer recognise as beliefs, and stay honest with colleagues and bosses. He frames the goal of security as keeping the world relatively stable rather than defeating a single adversary.

talks.title: TROOPERS11 - Adventures in SCADA
talks.teaser: Sergey Bratus investigates TROOPERS11 - Adventures in SCADA.

talks.title: TROOPERS11 - Milking a horse
talks.teaser: Walks through remote code execution bugs in Struts, Spring MVC and JBoss, and why Java's security manager falls short.
talks.summary:
The talk covers how modern Java web frameworks take over tasks like parameter conversion, validation and object construction, moving complexity into reflection-heavy framework code. Three popular frameworks were examined: Apache Struts, Spring MVC and JBoss Seam, each with a sample application.

In Struts, OGNL expressions submitted through form fields could be evaluated during validation, and a later bypass using a hex-escaped hash character reached session context and disabled method execution checks, leading to operating system command execution. The fix took about three months to ship because the release needed council votes. In Spring MVC, binding to the class loader path let an attacker point a tag library at a remote jar holding a tag file with code; the fix blacklisted that path. In JBoss Seam, an action outcome parameter interpolated expressions, and reflection to reach Runtime.exec gave command execution through a crafted URL.

The talk then examined Java's SecurityManager, which many teams skip because of its performance cost and its origins in untrusted applet code. The speaker proposed a lighter custom manager that focuses on file, socket, reflection and exec access, grants permissions by class name, and was released as open source. It would not stop logic abuse inside the application itself. Practitioners should review custom expression languages and reflection-based binding first, and use stop classes correctly.

talks.title: TROOPERS11 - I FOCA a MIL Domain
talks.teaser: Shows how metadata in public documents and websites can reveal internal users, printers and servers, using the FOCA tool.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces FOCA, a Windows tool that began as an internal utility for removing metadata from documents before they left the company. The speaker separates three layers it reads: metadata written into files, hidden data that applications store but do not show, and lost data such as internal links or content copied from other files. Examples include a 2003 Word document tied to Tony Blair's office and a PDF press note from an Anonymous member that revealed his name.

The middle of the talk shows how authors, printers, template paths and server names pulled from public files can be assembled into a map of internal users, folders, servers and IP addresses. In a demo, 100 documents from a US defence domain produced internal names and network details. The speaker then moves to the web-scanning side, which checks for insecure HTTP methods, directory listings, DNS zone transfers and certificate names. In a day-long run against a large government domain, the project reached almost 2,000 internal servers, more than 10,000 domains and over 40,000 URLs.

The talk closes with a comparison of search engines, which return different document counts for the same query, and a reminder that FOCA only collects information from public sources. The practical lesson is that documents and sites reveal far more than their authors intend, so metadata should be stripped before publishing and published files and web servers should be reviewed for leaks.

talks.title: TROOPERS11 - SAP GUI Hacking
talks.teaser: Shows how malicious servers, insiders and web pages can abuse SAP GUI features to compromise client machines and sessions.
talks.summary:
SAP GUI is the desktop client many organizations use to reach SAP back ends. It is closed source and can be scripted, which makes it a useful target. The talk, presented by Andreas Wiegenstein, groups the attacks by who is hostile: a malicious server, a malicious user at the client, or an outside web page. The speaker argues that companies focus on standard SAP settings and patches but often overlook risks in their own custom ABAP code.

In the server-side case, function modules such as WS_EXECUTE can run operating system commands on the client, and the GUI upload and download functions move files between server and client. In a live demo, a server changed a local text file, opened it in Notepad and created a user account on the client machine, all without a visible hint to the user. Newer SAP GUI 7.20 can restrict these functions, while older 7.10 needs additional measures. For the malicious-user case, a restricted account used a window tool to make read-only fields editable and sent text into the interface to start a transaction it was not authorized to run. The talk also showed cross-site scripting through an HTML control, and VBScript run inside the GUI to launch another transaction.

The final case, which the speaker called cross-application request forgery, showed that a file type downloaded in a browser could be opened by SAP GUI and push commands into an active session. A confirmation prompt blocked the demo action. SAP has patched the issue, but the talk stresses applying patches promptly. The takeaways are to avoid relying on data stored in disabled client controls, to handle input to HTML controls carefully, and to disable SAP GUI scripting where it is not needed.

talks.title: TROOPERS11 - Femtocell: Femtostep to the Holy Grail
talks.teaser: Shows how consumer femtocell boxes were rooted via flawed recovery and provisioning, exposing calls, SMS and operator servers.
talks.summary:
This talk by Ravishankar Borgaonkar and Kevin Redon examines femtocells, small home access points that connect phones to a mobile operator's 3G network over a broadband line. It covers where the boxes are sold or given away, why operators like them for offloading traffic, and why they were a rare chance to study cellular gear directly. The speakers also describe how operators try to tie each box to a location, and how the team got past IP, GPS and nearby-cell checks in a lab.

The core of the talk is the device analysis. The recovery procedure fetched its parameter list and firmware over HTTPS, yet the parameter list could be retrieved unencrypted by changing the URL, and the box did not authenticate the server. By posing as that server, the team supplied its own parameters, including the public key used to check images, and then loaded its own signed firmware. Switching a hardware flag from commercial to development mode produced a root login. A hidden web interface and a management server then exposed other boxes' configuration and subscriber data, and in open access mode traffic from phones that connected could be read.

The takeaway is that femtocells sit inside the operator's trust boundary, so a compromised box can expose calls, SMS and browsing. The speakers urged operators to follow the specification, using trusted hardware to protect credentials, and to tighten security and privacy controls on their management servers. Their work covered the access network only; the core network was not tested.

talks.title: TROOPERS10 - How to fail an audit
talks.teaser: Explains common ways ISO 27001 audits go wrong, from poor preparation and vague findings to uninformed management.
talks.summary:
The talk offers a short introduction to ISO 27001 and its audits, aimed at technically minded security people who may be unfamiliar with compliance work. The speaker argues that the standard is not a checklist of controls but a way for an organisation to decide what good security means for its business, where its risks lie, and how to manage security over time. Technology alone does not provide that overall view, so an outside auditor is needed to spot what insiders miss.

Much of the talk lists ways audits go wrong. Companies haggle over price, pick the cheapest auditor, and then treat the auditor as an enemy. Findings can be vague, such as an outdated web server with no version given, or contradictory, such as a backup concept reported as both existing and missing. Unprepared staff, missing documents, a cluttered data centre, or engineers who over-explain technical details all make the audit harder. Managers who do not understand security, and last-minute paperwork, add to the problem.

The speaker's takeaways are to plan audits early, brief staff on what to expect, train management so leaders understand their security obligations, and highlight what works as well as what does not. Findings should be handled through the year rather than crammed before the next visit, and disputes should go through formal channels rather than arguments with the auditor. Audits cost real money, so the talk argues they should deliver real value.

talks.title: TROOPERS09 - Stop the Madness
talks.teaser: Argues that disabling unneeded services and plugins cuts risk more cheaply than buying extra security appliances.
talks.summary:
This keynote, aimed at security officers in large organizations, argues that many programs put too much effort into detective and reactive controls and too little into prevention. The speaker frames the work as risk management under limited resources, sorting controls into preventive, detective and reactive types. A house of security built on three pillars, components, implementation and operations, is introduced, and the speaker suggests most organizations overweight buying products.

The middle of the talk looks at how malware usually reaches a system. The speaker argues that user-assisted paths through browsers and their plugins now matter more than network services, and that JavaScript, Flash, QuickTime and the Acrobat reader can often be disabled with little business cost. Windows GDI handling of EMF and WMF image files, tied to several remote code execution advisories, can be blocked by turning off metafile rendering with one registry key. Data Execution Prevention is presented as a simple setting which the speaker says made a widely published Internet Explorer exploit fail before a patch was available. An anecdote about a chief security officer who stopped a device control tool in Task Manager, which needed admin rights, illustrates why users should not work as administrators.

The closing message is that risk management comes first, prevention deserves more resources, and simple operational steps are often overlooked. In the Q&A, the speaker notes that patch management is a reactive control, and that limiting the attack surface is usually more cost effective.

talks.title: TROOPERS10 - Federated Identity - Opportunities and Dangers
talks.teaser: Compares enterprise and consumer federated identity protocols and the security pitfalls each one brings for application builders.
talks.summary:
The talk gives an overview of federated identity, the approach of letting a user reuse an account from their home domain in another application without copying accounts or passwords. It explains why this matters for enterprise software sold to customers and partners, and for consumer sites that want one login across many services. The enterprise side is framed around SAML and the WS-* protocol family built on security token services, while the consumer side is framed around OpenID and OAuth.

The walk-through covers how a browser-based SAML flow moves a signed, optionally encrypted token from an identity provider to the application through redirects, and how WS-Trust adds proof of possession using a session key. A live demo shows a token service issuing claims to an application, followed by a small bridge that takes an OpenID login and turns it into a WS-Federation token. Home realm discovery is raised as a design issue for multi-tenant applications that must decide where to send each user.

The security part focuses on risks. Tokens act as bearer credentials, so they need encryption, short lifetimes and replay checks, and browser flows depend heavily on SSL, which stripping attacks target. Phishing and cross-site request forgery become more attractive when one account opens many services. The takeaway is to adopt a proven vendor and a maintained library rather than implementing these protocols by hand, and to keep trust relationships tightly scoped.

talks.title: TROOPERS09 - .NET Access Control Service
talks.teaser: Explains Microsoft's cloud-hosted claims rules service and how it normalizes tokens for applications.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at Microsoft's Access Control Service, a resource security token service hosted in Microsoft's cloud that was not yet released when it was presented. Dominick Baier opens with why applications keep scattering their own user stores, and how Kerberos centralised sign-in but struggled across organisational boundaries. Token-based federation with WS-Federation, WS-Trust and SAML then lets an application trust one issuer and read user attributes from the token itself.

The middle section walks through the service. An administrator registers each application by its identifier, chooses an encryption key for outgoing tokens, and selects which identity providers to accept. A rules engine maps incoming claims to new output claims, and forward-chaining rules let one generated claim feed further rules, so an application only checks for a simple permission. Demos showed a plain copy rule, a Windows Live ID account mapped to a group, and a multilevel government-style clearance model built entirely from claim rules, where raising a clearance upstream changed which documents could be read.

The takeaway is that a resource STS can absorb differing partner claim names and keep application code simple. Removing someone from a partner's directory also ends their access, which is better than manual account provisioning. The speaker expects more security services to run off-premises, so practitioners should weigh whether to run this kind of infrastructure themselves or buy it as a service.

talks.title: TROOPERS13
talks.teaser: Explains why vulnerability severity ratings are hard and presents a new metric for prioritizing pentest findings.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a common problem for penetration testers: clients ask how critical a finding is, and a simple label rarely answers that. The presenters explain that they adopted CVSS in their reports around 2007-2008 because it was the only usable metric available then, even though it was designed for patch management. They walk the audience through a live CVSS v2 rating of a SQL injection in a web shop, and show how many answers depend on context, such as the attack vector, whether impact is partial or complete, and who fills in the environmental questions.

They also look at WSS, a weakness-scoring approach that is still at version 0.8, and at risk-based and custom scoring schemes used in large environments. Their criticism is that these schemes leave many parameters vague, rely on subjective factors, and see little ongoing development. Their own approach uses five categories: characteristics, exploitability, impact, mitigation effort and environment, combined through a weighted formula into a score. Rating the same SQL injection, then a variant on a public catalog, shows how a change in data classification moves the result to a lower, yellow-level rating.

The main takeaway is that metrics are hard, and the presenters describe their approach as a version 0.9 aimed at prioritizing directly exploitable vulnerabilities. Audit findings such as insufficient backups need a different treatment, and they say they have not solved that yet. They plan to release a free tool for Windows, macOS and Linux with a save function shortly after the conference, so that practitioners can test the approach on their own findings.

talks.title: TROOPERS13 - Understanding & Mitigating Large Scale DoS Attacks
talks.teaser: Explains the main types of denial-of-service attacks and why scrubbing, ACL automation and vendor claims often fall short.
talks.summary:
The talk traces how denial-of-service attacks grew from a side effect of early TCP/IP weaknesses into a mainstream threat driven by large botnets, with attacks reaching around 100 Gbit/s. The speaker groups real-world attacks into four major categories: application-layer attacks, protocol state attacks such as SYN floods, volumetric floods, and multi-vector combinations of these. Common tools such as hping and slow HTTP clients rely on brute force rather than vulnerabilities, and slow HTTP requests that are never completed can exhaust a server's sockets while showing little on the server itself.

The talk then challenges several myths. Lab tests are presented as showing that firewalls and IPS devices can fail under modest packet rates, regardless of vendor claims, and one vendor reportedly confirmed that its firewalls were vulnerable in default configuration. Cloud-based scrubbing raises certificate and data-protection concerns and creates a single point of failure. Automatically generated ACLs are shown to be risky, since a Cloudflare outage was linked to a rule matching oversized packets that was pushed across Juniper routers. Blackholing is described as no real mitigation, because the customer is still knocked offline.

For practitioners, the main takeaways are to combine purpose-built scrubbing with the ISP, collect NetFlow to learn normal traffic, apply rate limiting at the application layer, monitor server sockets, and test defences with traffic generators instead of trusting datasheets. Joining information-sharing groups and watching public announcements are presented as useful early warning sources.

talks.title: TROOPERS13 - Hacking & Defending the big 4 Databases
talks.teaser: Surveys attacks on Oracle, SQL Server, Sybase, and DB2, pairing live exploit demos with patching, privilege, and auditing guidance.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by arguing that most breached records live in databases and that perimeter controls alone leave crown-jewel data exposed once attackers reach the internal network. He frames recurring weaknesses—default credentials, weak access control, SQL injection, Java features, misconfiguration, and unpatched engines—against an informal top-ten list familiar from broader application security guidance.

The middle of the session walks through concrete escalation paths: SQL Server 2008 restore-time injection elevating a limited user; Sybase naming tricks that execute embedded SQL during index creation; Oracle PUBLIC Java permissions enabling OS commands; Sybase Java reflection loading arbitrary DLLs; Oracle MDSYS spatial procedure chains granting DBA; DB2 repeat-based denial of service; and TNS listener poisoning intercepting client traffic. Each demo stresses that flaws often sit in vendor code or risky optional components such as xp_cmdshell, OPENROWSET, or Enterprise Manager.

Closing guidance repeats a practitioner playbook: patch quickly across critical and forgotten instances, shrink installed features, grant least privilege through roles, audit logins and role membership, monitor for suspicious function use, encrypt data at rest and in transit, inventory every database instance, and assign clear ownership between DBAs, data owners, and security leadership.

talks.title: TROOPERS13 - You wouldn't share a syringe. Would you share a USB port?
talks.teaser: Shows how USB drivers trust whatever a device says, and how Python-built emulated devices can expose bugs in host stacks.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that USB ports deserve the same scrutiny as network ports. Host drivers accept what a device reports during enumeration, from descriptor lengths to later replies, and they often assume a device will stay consistent. The speaker presents Facedancer, a low-cost platform where a workstation drives the USB side through a controller chip and Python code, so it can act as almost any USB device with far more memory and logging than an embedded emulator offers.

Several case studies follow. A malformed HID descriptor is shown reaching a format string flaw in an X.org driver on older Linux kiosk systems, where a percent-n specifier allows writes to memory. Device-side bugs are covered as well, including weak firmware update protocols on cheap MP3 players, and a Samsung television jailbreak that relied on a mass storage device returning different file contents on repeated reads. Other examples show forensic tools being fingerprinted by an emulated disk that reacts to how a lab reads it, and platform differences where Windows auto-installs drivers, macOS has stack speed and driver limits, and FreeBSD needs drivers loaded explicitly.

The closing section argues that USB stacks should be mapped and fuzzed like network services, with the weakest endpoint found first. Practitioners should treat device-supplied values as untrusted, consider driver firewalls or user-land USB stacks, and in the meantime glue unused ports shut. The speaker notes that USB 3 is not yet supported by the tool.

talks.title: TROOPERS13 - OAuth2 - Ready or not (here I come)
talks.teaser: Walks through OAuth 2.0 flows and their weaknesses, from bearer tokens and redirect URIs to client binding and sign-in misuse.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who works with developers building internal and commercial software, explains OAuth 2.0 as an authorization protocol rather than an authentication one. He describes why it displaced the older WS-* specifications as mobile and roaming clients became common. Using a valet parking key analogy, he introduces the roles of resource owner, client, resource server and authorization server, then walks through the authorization code flow for web applications, the implicit flow for installed apps, and the resource owner password flow for trusted clients. Token formats, lifetimes and refresh tokens are covered along the way, including how revocation works.

The middle of the talk covers the protocol's history, from a single author who withdrew his name before finalization to the many revisions and satellite specifications that left much to implementers. The main criticisms are that bearer tokens are protected only by TLS, that carrier-branded certificates and disabled certificate validation in apps can expose them, and that redirect URIs are often checked loosely. He also shows how embedded login windows give users no real way to verify who is asking for their password, and how using OAuth as a sign-in mechanism let a malicious app pass a token to a legitimate one.

He concludes that the protocol itself is not the main problem, but its many options and loose implementations are, and that developers without security backgrounds are a risk when they implement it. For practitioners, the takeaways are to use OpenID Connect for authentication, validate redirect URIs strictly, bind refresh tokens to clients, and treat the specification as a set of pitfalls rather than a finished recipe.

talks.title: TROOPERS13 - Ghost in the Shell
talks.teaser: Shows how a logged-on SAP GUI user can send commands into other active sessions, forging audit logs and locking accounts.
talks.summary:
The two speakers, both SAP security researchers, present a new attack on SAP systems. They first explain why SAP matters: it runs business processes for many large companies, and its back end holds very large numbers of database tables and programs. Most back-end access by employees, administrators and developers still goes through SAP GUI, a proprietary client that can reach the local file system and carries all data between user and server. The talk also covers forensic controls. The security audit log and the system trace are usually not switched on by default, because they generate heavy storage use.

The demonstrations show an attacker on a second machine, logged into the same application server, making a victim's session run a program. The audit log then records that action under the victim's account, even though the victim never touched the machine. Further demos show the attacker listing other logged-on users, launching an arbitrary operating system command with parameters on a victim's machine, and creating and deleting a file there. In a live session, a volunteer's screen was blanked, and an editor session with unsaved work was killed, which also locked the user account.

The speakers contrast this with passive cross-site request forgery, which needs a planted trap and a waiting victim. This variant is active and targets sessions in real time. SAP has released a security note that fixes the issue, and a newer SAP GUI version prompts users before file creation or command execution. Practitioners should keep SAP patched, review custom programs that could trigger such mechanisms, and note that the attack also works across application servers if the attacker can reach them.

talks.title: TROOPERS13 - Virtual firewalls - the Good, the Bad and the Ugly
talks.teaser: A networking-focused survey weighs VM appliances, per-VM NIC firewalls, and service insertion trade-offs in virtualized estates.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames how firewalls moved from straightforward physical packet filters and stateful boxes into virtualization platforms, where most serious abuse still targets application layers while perimeter controls remain necessary hygiene. It contrasts virtual contexts on hardware appliances with true virtual firewalls on hypervisors, highlighting portability, disaster recovery, and tenant-managed policies alongside shared resources, noisy-neighbor effects, and hypervisor risk.

Four implementation paths dominate the middle: full VM appliances mirroring physical gear (with performance bounded by hypervisor and Linux TCP stacks unless bypassed), NIC-level filters in front of each workload (scaling capacity with the cluster but demanding a mindset shift away from VLAN-centric zones), and vendor-specific service insertion that hairpins traffic to external boxes—Cisco’s Nexus 1000V with virtual security gateway and adaptive security appliance combinations, Juniper’s kernel versus VM filtering, VMware vShield, and HP’s IDS-oriented redirection. Measurements cited range from roughly one gigabit per virtual CPU on naive stacks to far higher throughput when stacks or the hypervisor are removed from the path.

Practitioners are urged to match architecture to risk appetite and audit posture, accept added east-west traffic unless the fabric is non-oversubscribed, and ask vendors about statefulness, kernel versus VM filtering, control-plane failure modes, and multi-tenant operations. Closing notes emphasize that organizational silos and responsibility shifting often block adoption more than technology, with familiar CLI-centric designs sometimes easing political transitions.

talks.title: TROOPERS13 - Keynote Day 2 by Chris Nickerson
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of TROOPERS13 - Keynote Day 2 by Chris Nickerson.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Chris Nickerson's TROOPERS 13 keynote challenges conventional cybersecurity thinking by drawing parallels between historical military defeats of superpowers and modern security failures. Delivered in an informal, conversational style, the talk argues that defenders repeatedly lose not due to lack of resources or technology, but because they misunderstand the nature of the conflict and fail to secure their fundamental advantages.

## Key Historical Parallels
Nickerson uses historical examples to frame security strategy: the Scythians defeating the Persian Empire, Britons against Romans, the Tanguts resisting Mongol domination, and Spanish guerrilla fighter Juan Martín Díez Porlier leading a seven-person force against French military might. The common thread: smaller, motivated forces that understand their environment defeat larger, better-equipped adversaries through tactical knowledge and will rather than raw resources. The talk directly applies this to modern cybersecurity: defenders possess more resources but systematically lose strategic advantages.

## Core Problems Identified
1. **Misplaced Focus**: Organizations prioritize installing technology and achieving compliance checkboxes rather than understanding their business operations and actual adversaries.
2. **False Security**: Compliance standards provide arbitrary metrics unrelated to actual business protection. Sophisticated controls increase attack surface complexity while often remaining vulnerable to simple, decades-old techniques.
3. **User Blame**: Security professionals blame users for being "stupid" rather than recognizing unrealistic expectations placed on non-security staff.
4. **Lack of Testing**: Organizations rarely verify that installed controls actually function as intended, creating false confidence in their security posture.
5. **Disconnection from Business**: Security teams don't understand how their companies generate revenue or operate, making their defensive strategies ineffective.

## Technical and Strategic Insights
- **Defense Formula**: Defense = Capability + Experience (not technology quantity)
- **Home Field Advantage**: Defenders give away their inherent advantage by not understanding their environment
- **Attack Surface**: Every control added increases complexity and attack surface; security professionals must evaluate trade-offs
- **Physical Security**: Social engineering and physical attacks often bypass technical defenses
- **Vendor Solutions**: Security vendors profit by selling solutions to compliance-driven security postures rather than solving actual problems

## Methodology and Solutions
Nickerson advocates for attack modeling based on specific adversaries rather than generic penetration testing. Organizations should:
- Interview executives to understand business objectives and operations
- Profile actual adversaries rather than conducting theoretical assessments
- Test all defensive implementations to confirm effectiveness
- Frame security through disaster-recovery economics (quantifying downtime costs)
- Create achievable goals that make companies "addicted to progress"
- Practice basic security fundamentals flawlessly rather than implementing advanced but untested controls
- Understand company mission statements and align security around business protection, not compliance

## Key Takeaways
- **Security is not about technology accumulation** but about understanding your business and environment
- **Education matters more than controls**: Training people through realistic adversarial experiences prevents panic during actual attacks (referencing Mike Tyson's quote: "everybody has a plan until they get punched in the face")
- **Stop blaming users**: Unrealistic security expectations placed on non-security staff reflect poor security design
- **All organizations have been compromised**: This should motivate progress, not despair
- **Measure security by business survival**: If the company operates profitably and hasn't been materially compromised, defensive objectives were met
- **Adopt home field advantage**: Defenders who understand their terrain defeat better-resourced attackers

talks.title: TROOPERS13 - Paparazzi over IP
talks.teaser: Shows how a networked Canon camera can be sniffed, spoofed, and taken over through its FTP, DLNA, web and PTP/IP modes.
talks.summary:
This talk examines the network features of a high-end Canon EOS camera, which has an Ethernet port and an optional wireless file transmitter. The speakers argue that these features open new attack paths, because anyone on the same network segment as a camera at an event or in a hotel can reach it. They began at the lower layers: ARP spoofing against the camera worked easily, and around 100 ARP packets per second was enough to deny service to its network stack. Forged TCP reset packets also tore down its connections.

The camera offers four communication modes: FTP upload, DLNA, a built-in web server, and the EOS Utility mode. In FTP mode, credentials and images travel in plain text, so a man-in-the-middle can capture passwords and recover every uploaded JPEG with standard command-line tools. DLNA has no authentication, so any client can browse and download stored media. The web server uses a four-byte session ID, which the speakers brute forced in about 18 to 20 minutes, after which they reached the storage, camera settings and live view. The EOS Utility mode relies on PTP/IP, and its pairing step accepts any credentials while the camera is in pairing mode. The 16-byte GUID needed to authenticate was broadcast by the camera over UPnP in obfuscated form, and a short script recovered it. Because the camera allows only one connection at a time, the speakers reset the legitimate client, connected themselves, and downloaded images during a live demo.

The talk closes with limited countermeasures: keep the network functions disabled unless needed, and use only trusted networks with encryption. The speakers note that the same classic attacks keep working against connected consumer devices, and that newer models with built-in access points are next on their list.

talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning TROOPERS13 - Keynote Day 1 by Rodrigo Branco.
talks.summary: Rodrigo Branco opens Troopers with a provocative critique of how the security industry researches vulnerabilities yet fails against malware and nation-state campaigns. He challenges APT attribution reports, questions whether breaches are truly advanced, and argues antivirus economics discourage real fixes. Branco contrasts mature vulnerability markets with immature anti-malware science, calls out academia's distance from deployments, and proposes theories meant to spark debate rather than prescribe answers. The keynote mixes philosophy, historical breach anecdotes, and Brazilian humor while urging practitioners to revisit assumptions about expertise, economics, and threat labels.

talks.title: TROOPERS13 - Your IPv6 default config meets FOCA (...and starts to cry)
talks.teaser: Shows how default IPv6 settings in Windows let an attacker intercept local network traffic through rogue router advertisements.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a simple point: IPv6 is enabled by default on Windows machines since Vista, even on networks where administrators never configured it. Windows prefers IPv6 for connections on the local segment and tries IPv6 name resolution first. Most network defences are built around ARP and IPv4, so the speaker argues they miss the equivalent IPv6 traffic, where Neighbor Discovery takes over the role ARP plays.

The demonstrations begin with neighbor advertisement spoofing, which places an attacker between a client and a Windows file server so that the file share session can be captured and read. The central case is a rogue router. By sending Router Advertisement messages, an attacker makes a Windows host configure it as the default gateway and, through default DNS discovery, as its DNS server. A client on a network with only a link-local IPv4 address then depends on the attacker, whose translation tool converts IPv6 requests into IPv4 requests for sites that have no IPv6 records. In the demo, HTTPS links were downgraded to HTTP and the credentials typed into a login form were captured. The talk also describes a denial-of-service in which repeated Router Advertisements make Windows create many addresses until its memory is exhausted, and notes that the vendor's only advice is to filter these messages on switches.

The takeaways are that IPv6 is present on most networks whether or not it was configured, that disabling it can break services that depend on it, and that IPv4-focused security tooling needs IPv6 coverage to be useful.

talks.title: TROOPERS13 - Introducing Daisho
talks.teaser: Introduces Daisho, an open source modular hardware platform for monitoring and injecting traffic on high-speed wired links.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Daisho, a project by Michael Ossmann and Dominic Spill with teammates, aimed at monitoring and manipulating wired communication at the physical layer. The speakers argue that wireless protocols only became well understood once practical tools let researchers examine them from the bottom up, and they want the same for high-speed wired links such as gigabit Ethernet, USB 3.0, HDMI and RS-232. They describe why existing options fall short: passive taps only handle slower Ethernet, switch mirror ports are visible to the target network, software captures sit too high in the stack, and affordable USB and HDMI monitors are closed, limited or lack buffering.

A key problem is the bottleneck where a full-duplex gigabit tap feeds a one-direction gigabit link to the laptop. Their answer is a main board with an FPGA, RAM and a USB 3.0 link to the host, with PHY chips wired straight to the FPGA, so traffic can be buffered, sent to Wireshark, or altered in line. Swappable front-end modules carry each medium. An RS-232 module was demonstrated passing serial data while tapped, and an HDMI module is planned, though Ethernet over HDMI is unsupported until its specification is available.

Software centers on a host library for USB transfers and Wireshark plugins, and all hardware and software is to be open source on GitHub. Thunderbolt was judged hard to support for now, while PCI Express and DMA attacks were presented as areas of interest. The project is funded by DARPA's Cyber Fast Track program, and the speakers invited third-party front ends that extend the platform.
